parole.testo: From Old Norse bœta, from Proto-Germanic *bōtijaną.
From Old Norse bíta, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).
From Old Norse bíða, from Proto-Germanic *bīdaną. The irregular supine beðið is probably the result of contamination with the verb biðja (“to bid”).

From Old Norse bófi (“boy”), from Proto-Germanic *bōbô, from *bō- (“close [male] relation”). Cognate with Dutch boef (“mischievous boy, rascal; also thief”), Middle Low German bôve, German Bube (“boy, rascal, knave, rogue”), dialectal Swedish babbe (“little boy”) and English bub.

parole.significato: a shoulder of an animal, especially as meat
parole.testo: From Old Norse bógr, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz.
From Old Norse bók, from Proto-Germanic *bōks.
From Old Norse bókstafr, from Proto-Germanic *bōkastabaz, equivalent to bók (“book”) + stafur (“letter, character”).
From Old Norse ból, from Proto-Germanic *bōþlą.
From Old Norse bólstr, bulstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz. Compare Swedish and Norwegian bolster, Dutch bolster, German Polster, English bolster.
From Old Norse bón (“prayer, petition”), from Proto-Germanic *bōniz (“supplication”). Related to boon (“good, favorable”, adjective); see there for more.

Inherited from Old Norse bót, from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“recompense”). Cognates include Old Swedish bōt (“improvement”) whence Swedish bot (“fine”). Compare also Bót- in the names Bótey, Bóthildur and Bótólfur, Swedish Boel and Bodil and Danish Bodil. Related to Proto-Germanic *batiz (“good; better
From Old Norse bǫl (“bale, misfortune”), from Proto-Germanic *balwą.

From Old Norse bǫllr (“ball, globe; glans penis”), from Proto-Germanic *balluz (“ball”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“a bubble”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, to inflate, to swell”); compare English ball. For the semantic evolution, compare Swedish balle.
From Old Norse bǫrkr, from Proto-Germanic *barkuz.
From Old Norse búa, from Proto-Germanic *būaną.
From Old Norse búkr, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz.
From Old Norse búr, from Proto-Germanic *būrą (“cabin, hut”), cognate with English bower and German Bauer (“birdcage”).
From Old Norse bútr, from Proto-Germanic *butaz, *buttaz.
From Old Norse búð, a variant of *bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, dwelling”).
From Old Norse bý, from Proto-Germanic *bijō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰī-.
From Old Norse býsn, from Proto-Germanic *būsniz.
From Old Norse dafna, from Proto-Germanic *dabanōną, from Proto-Germanic *dabaną (“to be fitting”).

parole.significato: Dane (a person from Denmark or of Danish descent)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse danir, from Proto-Germanic *daniz.
From Old Norse dapr, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz, whence also Old High German tapfar.
From Old Norse daufr, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-.
From Old Norse daunn, from Proto-Germanic *dauniz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰowh₂-nis, from the root *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist, haze”). Cognate with English dain.
From Old Norse dauði, dauðr, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz.
From Old Norse dauðr, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz.
From Old Norse deig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, to mold, to form”). Compare Faroese deiggj, Norwegian Bokmål deig, Swedish deg, Danish dej.
From Old Norse deigja, from Proto-Germanic *daigijǭ (“dairy maid, bread kneader”).
From Old Norse deigr, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz.
From Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną.

parole.significato: to kill, to put to death
parole.testo: From Old Norse deyða, from Proto-Germanic *daudijaną.
From Old Norse digr, from Proto-Germanic *digraz.

parole.significato: a suckling lamb, a lamb at springtime
parole.testo: From Old Norse dilkr, from Proto-Germanic *dilkaz, related to *dajjaną, *dēaną, *dijōną (“suckle”) and *delō (“nipple”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Originally referred to the young of any livestock (sheep, goats, horses, pigs or cattle) that are bein
From Old Norse dylja, from Proto-Germanic *dilja-, of uncertain, non-Indo-European origin, possibly a substrate.
From Old Norse dimmr, from Proto-Germanic *dimmaz. Cognate with Old English dimm (whence English dim).
From Old Norse djarfr, from Proto-Germanic *derbaz.
From Old Norse djúpr, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-.

parole.significato: to go numb, to become numb
parole.testo: From Old Norse dofna, from Proto-Germanic *dubnaną.
From Old Norse draga, from Proto-Germanic *draganą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ-.
From Old Norse draugr, from Proto-Germanic *draugaz.
From Old Norse draumr, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz.
From Old Norse dregg (“sediment”), from Proto-Germanic *dragjō, whence also Middle English dreg (> English dregs). Replaced Old English dræst and dærst.
From Old Norse dreif (“a scattering, spread”), from Proto-Germanic *draibō (“a driving”), from Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”).
From Old Norse dreifa, from Proto-Germanic *draibijaną.
From Old Norse drekka, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną.
From Old Norse drekkja, from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną.

parole.significato: to cause to dream [with preceding accusative ‘experiencer’, along with following accusative ‘thing dreamed’ or um (+ ac…
parole.testo: From Old Norse dreyma, from Proto-Germanic *draumijaną. Compare Danish drøm, Faroese droyma, English dream.

From Old Norse dreyri, from Proto-Germanic *drauzijô. Cognate with Old Saxon drōr, Old High German trōr and Old English dreor. The historical sense is of something which ‘falls’: the Germanic base is also the source of Old English drēosan (“fall”), English dreary.
From Old Norse drit, from Proto-Germanic *dritą.
From Old Norse drjúgr, from Proto-Germanic *dreugaz.

parole.significato: to drip, to fall in drops
parole.testo: From Old Norse drjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *dreupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrew-.
From Old Norse dropi, from Proto-Germanic *drupô.
From Old Norse drykkr (“a drink”), from Proto-Germanic *drunkiz, whence also Old English drync and Old High German trunch. Cognate with Danish drink and Swedish dryck.
From Old Norse drynja, from Proto-Germanic *drunjaną (“to rumble”).
From Old Norse dráttr, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz. Derived from the ancestor of the verb draga (“drag”). Compare English draught.

From Old Norse drífa, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”). Compare Faroese dríva, Danish and Norwegian drive, Swedish driva, English drive, Dutch drijven, German treiben.

From Old Norse drýgja, from Proto-Germanic *driugijaną, derived from *dreugaz (“long-lasting”), in the sense “eke out”. The sense “commit” may be carried over from the related strong verb *dreuganą (whence Old English drēogan (“to perform (a duty)”), Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (driugan, “to perform military ser
From Old Norse dupt, from Proto-Germanic *duftaz. Cognate with Danish duft, Swedish doft, German Duft (“smell”).
From Old Norse duga (“to help, to suffice”), from Proto-Germanic *duganą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to produce”).
From Old Norse dulr, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz (“stunned, confused”).
From Old Norse dvala, dvalan, from Proto-Germanic *dwalaz (“stunned, confused”). Related to Old Norse dvelja (“to remain, stay, to delay”).

parole.significato: to stay, to remain, to dwell
parole.testo: From Old Norse dvelja (“to remain, stay, to delay”), from Proto-Germanic *dwaljaną (“to be stunned, confused”).
From Old Norse dvergr, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz.
From Old Norse dvína, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną. Compare English dwine, dwindle, Dutch verdwijnen, Low German verdwienen.
From Old Norse dygð (“virtue”) (cognate with Norwegian, Swedish dygd, Danish dyd), from Proto-Germanic *dugiþō, a variant of *dugunþō; compare English douth, German Tugend, Dutch deugd.

From Old Norse dylgja (“enmity, hostility”), to the same root as dólgur (“bully”), from Old Norse dolgr (“enemy”), originally from a Proto-Germanic *dula stem, an ablaut biform to the stem of Icelandic dvali, Swedish dvala (“dormancy”). Cognate to Old Swedish dylghia (“enmity”), Swedish döddölja, dö
From Old Norse dylja, from Proto-Germanic *duljaną.

parole.significato: to resound, to boom, to reverberate
parole.testo: From Old Norse dynja, from Proto-Germanic *dunjaną (“to rumble, make a roaring sound”).
From Old Norse dyntr, from Proto-Germanic *duntiz. Cognate with English dent, dint.
From Old Norse dyrr, from Proto-Germanic *duriz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door, gate”).
From Old Norse dyrvǫrðr, dyravǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *durawardaz. Equivalent to dyr + vörður.
From Old Norse dyrgja, from Proto-Germanic *durgijǭ. Related to dvergur (“dwarf”).

parole.significato: pile of rocks used to bury a dead body; cairn
parole.testo: From Old Norse dys (“grave mound”), from an earlier Proto-Germanic *dusjō-.
From Old Norse dá (“trance, senseless state”), from Proto-Germanic *dawą (“trance”), a nominal formation related to Etymology 2.
From Old Norse dá (“to admire”), from Proto-Germanic *dawāną (“to marvel”).
From Old Norse dálkr, from Proto-Germanic *dalkaz. Cognate with Old English dalc, dolc (“buckle, clasp, brooch, bracelet”).
From Old Norse dáð, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis.
From Old Norse dæla (“a small dale, ship's drain or pump, a small bucket, a groove, trough, trench, eaves”), from Proto-Germanic *dalą (“valley”). Cognate with both senses of English dale.
Inherited from Old Norse dæld, from Proto-Germanic *daliþō. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål deld, Norwegian Nynorsk dæld, and Swedish däld.
From Old Norse dæll, from Proto-Germanic *dēlijaz.
From Old Norse dǿma, from Proto-Germanic *dōmijaną.
From Old Norse dǿmi, from Proto-Germanic *dōmiją.
From Old Norse díki (compare English dike), from Proto-Germanic *dīkiją, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (whence also English ditch).
Inherited from Old Norse dís (“goddess”), from Proto-Germanic *dīsiz (“goddess”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“holy one, hallow, deity”).
From Old Norse dómr, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz.
From Old Norse dǫgg (“dew”), from Proto-Germanic *dawwō (“dew, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Cognate with Danish dug (“dew”).
From Old Norse dǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *dankō, *dankwō.
From Old Norse døkkr, dǫkkr, from Proto-Germanic *dankwaz. Cognates include Faroese døkkur and German dunkel.
From Old Norse dúfa, from Proto-Germanic *dūbǭ. Compare Faroese dúgva, Danish due, Norwegian Bokmål due, Swedish duva, Dutch duif, German Taube, English dove.
From Old Norse dúnn, from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz (“down”). Related to daunn (“unpleasant smell”).

parole.significato: to be compelled to stay; to loiter, hang about, often against one's will
parole.testo: From Old Norse dúsa, from Proto-Germanic *dusāną.

From Old Norse dý, related to dýja (“to shake, tremble”), from Proto-Germanic *dūjan- (“to tremble”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist”). Cognate with Faroese dýggj, Swedish dy, Danish dynd.
From Old Norse dýfa (“push down, dip”), from Proto-Germanic *dūbijaną. Compare Old English dȳfan (English dive).
From Old Norse dýpð, from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō, cognate with Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌹𐌸𐌰 (diupiþa) and English depth. Related to the Icelandic djúpur (“deep”).
From Old Norse dýrr from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz, whence also Old English dīere (English dear), Old High German tiuri. Cognates with Danish dyr, Faroese dýrur, Norwegian Bokmål dyr and Swedish dyr.
From Old Norse dýr, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą. Cognate with Faroese dýr, Danish dyr, Swedish djur, Old English dēor (> English deer), Old High German tior (> German Tier).
From Old Norse dýrð, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō. Cognates include Faroese dýrd and Swedish dyrd.
From Old Norse ef, from Proto-Germanic *jabai.
From Old Norse efja, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ (“ebb”). Cognate with English ebb.
From Old Norse efna, from Proto-Germanic *abnijaną.
From Old Norse efni, from Proto-Germanic *abniją. Cognate with Faroese evni, Danish evne, Norwegian Nynorsk emne, Swedish ämne.

From Old Norse eptir, eptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftiri (“more aft, further behind”), *after, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epóteros (“further behind, further away”), comparative form of *h₂epó (“off, behind”).
From Old Norse egg, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm. Cognate with Old English ǣġ (obsolete English ey); Swedish ägg; Old High German ei (German Ei).

parole.significato: the sharp edge of a knife, sword, or similar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse egg, from Proto-Germanic *agjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Cognates include Old Frisian egg, Old Saxon eggia, Dutch egge; Old English ecg (English edge); Old High German egga (German Ecke); Swedish egg. The Indo-European root is also the source of La
Inherited from Old Norse egna, from Proto-Germanic *agnijaną. Causative of agn (“bait”).
From Old Norse ei. A clipping of eigi, from Proto-Germanic *ni aiw-gin (“never”), from *ne, *ni (“not”) + *aiw (“always, for ever”) + *-gin. Not related to Finnish ei (“no”).

parole.significato: to have, to be closely related to
parole.testo: From Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aiganą.
From Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aigǭ, from the verb *aiganą.
From Old Norse eik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”).
From Old Norse eimr, from Proto-Germanic *aimaz. Cognate with Faroese eimur, Norwegian eim.
From Old Norse eimyrja, from Proto-Germanic *aimuzjǭ.
From Old Norse einfaldr, from Proto-Germanic *ainafalþaz (“onefold, simple”).

From Old Norse einka- and einka (“especially, exceptionally”, adverb). Probably a petrified genitive plural of an unattested noun Old Norse *eink f, from which there are also a petrified genitive singular einkar (“very”, adverb) and dative plural einkum (“especially”, adverb). This noun is possibly
From Old Norse einn, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos. Cognates include Norwegian Bokmål en, Faroese ein and Danish en.
Dative of eitt (“one”) sinn n (“time”). Inherited from Old Norse einu sinni (“once, sometime”), from Proto-Germanic *ainamai sinþai. Compare Gothic ainamma sinþa (“once”).

parole.significato: copper (a reddish-brown, malleable, ductile metallic element with high electrical and thermal conductivity, symbol Cu,…
parole.testo: From Old Norse eir, from Proto-Germanic *aiz. Cognate with Faroese eir, Norwegian eir, Danish ir, Old English ār (> English ore), Old High German ēr.
From Old Norse eitill, from or related to Proto-Germanic *aita- (“ulcer”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyd- (“to swell”), see also Latin aemidus.
From Old Norse eitra, from Proto-Germanic *aitrōną (“to fester, putrify, poison”).
From Old Norse eið, in turn from Proto-Germanic *aidiją, probably related to Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“go”) and Latin eo.
From Old Norse eiðr, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *oyt-. Cognate with English oath.
From Old Norse ekki, from Proto-Germanic *inkô.
From Old Norse ekkja, from Proto-Germanic *ainakjǭ, related to Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌺𐌻𐍃 (ainakls, “alone”).
From Old Norse elfr, from Proto-Germanic *albī.
From Old Norse elgr, from Proto-Germanic *algiz.
From Old Norse eljan, from Proto-Germanic *aljaną. Cognate with Old English ellen (“strength, courage”).
From Old Norse elja (“rival wife”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aljaną (“zeal, eagerness”). Cognate with Faroese eljustrið, Old High German ella, giella (“rival, mistress”).
From Old Norse ella, shortened from earlier elligar. Compare ellegar. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aljaz.
From Old Norse ellifu, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Compare Faroese ellivu, Norwegian and Danish elleve, Swedish elva.
From Old Norse elli, from Proto-Germanic *alþį̄.

parole.significato: to chase (to pursue, to follow at speed)
parole.testo: From Old Norse elta (“to chase, hunt, knead”), from Proto-Germanic *alatjaną (“to drive, move”).
From Old Norse embætti, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtiją.
From Old Norse emja (“to howl”), from Proto-Germanic *amjōną. Compare Old Norse emjar (“a part of a sword”, plural).
From Old Norse endalauss, from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz. Equivalent to endir + -laus. Cognate with Danish endeløs, Swedish ändlös and English endless.
From Old Norse endi, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.
From Old Norse endir, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.
From Old Norse endr, from Proto-Germanic *andiz.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter N/n.
parole.testo: From Old Norse enn, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.
From Old Norse enni, from Proto-Germanic *anþiją.
From Old Norse epli, from Proto-Germanic *apaliją, *apluz (“apple, fruit”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.
From Old Norse er, from Proto-Germanic *iz (“he”), from Proto-Indo-European *ís (“he, that”).
From Old Norse erfa, from Proto-Germanic *arbijaną, denominative from *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“change allegiance or status or ownership”). Cognate with Swedish ärva.
From Old Norse erfiði, erfaði, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiją.
From Old Norse *ergja, from Proto-Germanic *argijaną.
From Old Norse erendi, from Proto-Germanic *airundiją. Cognate with Danish ærinde, Swedish ärende, English errand.
From Old Norse ørlendr, erlendr, from Proto-Germanic *uzlandijaz.
From Old Norse ermr, from Proto-Germanic *armijō.
From Old Norse ern, from Proto-Germanic *arniz (“serious; diligent”).

parole.significato: to irritate (cause physical discomfort to a part of the body, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse erta, from Proto-Germanic *artijaną. More at ert.
From Old Norse ertr, from Proto-Germanic *arwīts. Cognate with Faroese ertur, Swedish ärt, Danish ært, Old High German arawīz (> German Erbse, Luxembourgish Ierbes).
From Old Norse eta, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.
From Old Norse etja, from Proto-Germanic *atjaną, from Pre-Germanic *h₃odéyeti, causative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to hate”).
Derived from Old Norse ey, from Proto-Germanic *awjō.
From Old Norse eygja, from Proto-Germanic *augijaną.
From older ey (dative eyju), from Old Norse ey, from Proto-Germanic *awjō.
From Old Norse eyland, from Proto-Germanic *awjōlandą. Equivalent to ey + land.
From Old Norse eyra, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ous-.
From Old Norse eyða, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaną. Related to the adjective auðr (“empty, barren”) ( > Icelandic auður).
From Old Norse eða, from Proto-Germanic *efþau and thus related to Old High German odar, Old English oþþe, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau).
From Old Norse eðli, from Proto-Germanic *aþulijaz.
From Old Norse eðr, from Proto-Germanic *efþau and thus related to Old High German odar, Old English oþþe, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau).
From Old Norse fagna, from Proto-Germanic *faginōną.
From Old Norse fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂ḱ- (“to fasten, place”).
From Old Norse falla, from Proto-Germanic *fallaną, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃lH-.

parole.significato: a socket at the back of a spearhead, into which the shaft is placed
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse falr, from Proto-Germanic *falhuz.
From Old Norse fang (“catch; embrace, hold (in wrestling)”), from Proto-Germanic *fangą (“catch”), from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną (“to take, to seize; to catch, to capture”).
From Old Norse fara, from Proto-Germanic *faraną, from Proto-Indo-European *por- (“going, passage”).
From Old Norse farmr, from Proto-Germanic *farmaz, from the strong verb *faraną (“to go”). Also see fara (“to go”).

From Old Norse farþegi, from far (“passage”) + *þegi, from the Proto-Germanic components *farą (“passing, passage”) and *þegô (“receiver”) respectively; the original meaning was thus “one who takes a passage”.
From Old Norse fasta, from Proto-Germanic *fastāną.
From Old Norse fasta, from Proto-Germanic *fastǭ.
From Old Norse fastr, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz.
From Old Norse fat, from Proto-Germanic *fatą, from Proto-Indo-European *pod-.
From Old Norse fata, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną (“to seize, hold”). Cognate with Jamtish futu.

Apparently a compound of Old Norse fat (“clothing”) (itself from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“clothes”)) + an element naður of unclear interpretation and origin (as the usual sense of "adder" or "sword" makes little sense in context).

From Old Norse faðir (“father”), from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr. Cognate with English father, German Vater, German Low German Vader, Voder, Vadder, Faroese faðir, Norwegian Bokmål far, fader, Norwegian Nynorsk far, fader, Danish far, fader, Swedish far, fader.
From Old Norse faðma, from the noun faðmr (“embrace, fathom”) (whence Modern Icelandic faðmur), from Proto-Germanic *faþmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-.
From Old Norse faðmr, from Proto-Germanic *faþmaz.
From Old Norse fegrð, from Proto-Germanic *fagriþō.

parole.significato: fey, doomed to death; fated to die, bound by death, death-bound
parole.testo: From the synonymous Old Norse feigr, from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz. Cognates include Old High German feigi (German feige (“cowardly”)); Old English fǣge (English fey) and Dutch veeg. Compare feig.

parole.significato: feyness, an approaching death or approach of death, imminent death, a foreboding of death
parole.testo: From Old Norse feigð, from Proto-Germanic *faigiþō. Equivalent to feigur + -ð.
From Old Norse feikn, from Proto-Germanic *faikną (“malice; deceit”), from Proto-Indo-European *peyǵ-.
From Old Norse feitr, from Proto-Germanic *faitaz.
From Old Norse fela, from Proto-Germanic *felhaną.
From Old Norse feldr, from Proto-Germanic *faldiz.
From Old Norse fella, from Proto-Germanic *fallijaną. Causative of falla (“to fall”).
From Old Norse fen, from Proto-Germanic *fanją.
From Old Norse fengr, from Proto-Germanic *fangiz.
From Old Norse fer-, from Proto-Germanic *feþur-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥-, the zero-grade form of *kʷetwóres (“four”).
From Old Norse fergja, from Proto-Germanic *fargijaną.

parole.significato: to load, to lade (e.g. a boat)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ferma (“to load, to lade”), from Proto-Germanic *fermōną. Compare Old English feormian (“to sustain, to feed; to entertain, to receive”).
From Old Norse ferskr, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz.
From Old Norse ferð, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz.
From Old Norse ferðask, from Proto-Germanic *fardijōną.
Inherited from Old Norse fet, from Proto-Germanic *fetą, from Proto-Indo-European *pedóm, from *ped-.
From Old Norse feyja, from Proto-Germanic *fawjaną.

From Old Norse feðgin (“father and mother; father and daughter”), derived from Proto-Germanic *fadrigaz (literally “paternal”) + *-īnaz (“made from”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, feðgar (“father and son; parents”) + -inn (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: skin, fishskin (especially with a layer of fat)
parole.testo: From Old Norse filla. Related to Proto-Germanic *fellą.

From Old Norse fimbul- inturn from the Proto-Germanic *fimfilaz. Compare Old English fīfel ("mighty, giant, great"), German Fimmel (“an iron wedge”) (whence Czech fimol), Swedish fimmelstång (“the handle of a sledgehammer”).
From Old Norse fimm (“five”), from Proto-Germanic *fimf. Cognates include Faroese fimm and Danish fem.
From Old Norse fimmti, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô.
From Old Norse fimmtán, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun.
From Old Norse fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz, from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷrós.
From Old Norse finna, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path, bridge”).
From Old Norse finnr, fiðr. Of unknown origin, but possibly from Proto-Germanic *fenþnōz pl (“wanderers, nomads”). Cognate with Faroese finnur and Norwegian finn.
From Old Norse firra, from Proto-Germanic *firrijaną.
From Old Norse fiska (“to fish”), from Proto-Germanic *fiskōną. Corresponds to fiskur m (“fish”) + -a (denominal suffix).
From Old Norse fiskr, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.
From Old Norse fiðla, from Proto-Germanic *fiþulǭ.

From Old Norse fiðrildi from the older term fífrildi, from Proto-Germanic *fifaldǭ *fīfildǭ (“butterfly”), from Proto-Indo-European *pāpel-, *pe(i)pel- (“butterfly”). The term fiðrildi came through the folk etymology that it was related to the Old Norse word fiðri (“feathers”) (compare the more mode
From Old Norse fiðri, from Proto-Germanic *fiþriją. Cognate with German Gefieder (“plumage”). Related to fjöður (“feather; spring”).
From Old Norse fjall, Proto-Germanic *falisaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pels-.
From Old Norse fjándi, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz. Cognate with Norwegian and Swedish fiende, Danish fjende, English fiend, Dutch vijand, German Feind.
From Old Norse fjórir, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr. Cognates include Faroese fýra and Danish fire.
From Old Norse fjórtán, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun.
From Old Norse fjórði, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþô.
From Old Norse fjórðungr, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþungaz, related to Icelandic fjórði (“fourth”).
From Old Norse fjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *felō.

From Old Norse fjǫl-, from Proto-Germanic *felu, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (the Indo-European root is also the source of Ancient Greek πολύς (polús), Latin plus (“more”), Ossetian фыр (fyr, “much”), Old Irish il, from whence the Welsh lliaws). Cognate with Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌻𐌿 (filu), Old High German
From Old Norse fjǫr, from Proto-Germanic *ferhwą, *ferhwō.
From Old Norse fjǫrðr (“firth, fjord”), from Proto-Germanic *ferþuz (“inlet, fjord”), from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”).
From Old Norse fjǫðr (“feather”), from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”).

parole.significato: to be drifted by the wind; to be blown away
parole.testo: From Old Norse fjúka, from Proto-Germanic *feukaną.

parole.significato: area of ground stripped of turf
parole.testo: From Old Norse flag, flaga, probably from Proto-Germanic *flaką (“something flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”). However, compare Proto-Germanic *plaggą.
From Old Norse flaga, flak, from Proto-Germanic *flakǭ, variant of *flaką (“something flat”), possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”).
From Old Norse flakka, from Proto-Germanic *flakkōną (“to flutter, wander, roam”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-, which could be related to Ancient Greek πλάζω (plázō, “to turn away from”).

parole.significato: to act rashly, get into something heedlessly, to rush
parole.testo: From Old Norse flana, possibly from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Borrowed into French as flâner (“to loiter, waste time”).

From Old Norse flasa, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *plē- (“to cut off, split off”), probably related to *pleh₂- (“flat”) and thus English flake, along with Faroese fles (“skerry”).
From Old Norse flaska, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of fíaskó.
From Old Norse flatr, from Proto-Germanic *flataz. Compare English flat, Swedish flat, Danish flad.
From Old Norse flaumr, from Proto-Germanic *flaumaz.
From Old Norse flekkr, from Proto-Germanic *flekka-. Cognate with Swedish fläck, Norwegian flekk, German Fleck, English fleck, Dutch vlek.
From Old Norse flengja, from Proto-Germanic *flangijaną, nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-.
From Old Norse flesk, from Proto-Germanic *flaiski, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁ḱ- (“to tear, peel off”).
From Old Norse fletja, from Proto-Germanic *flatjaną.

parole.significato: to peel, strip, remove a (thin) outer layer
parole.testo: From Old Norse fletta, ultimately from the source of Proto-Germanic *splītaną (“to split”).
From Old Norse fley, from Proto-Germanic *flawją.
From Old Norse fleygja, from Proto-Germanic *flaugijaną, causative of Proto-Germanic *fleuganą.

From Old Norse fleygr, from Proto-Germanic *flaugijaz, variant of *flugjaz. Compare Old English *flycge, attested in unflycge (“flightless”) (English fledge (“able to fly”)), Middle Low German vlugge, Old High German flucki (Middle High German vlücke).
From Old Norse fleygr, from Proto-Germanic *flaugiz.
From Old Norse fljót, from Proto-Germanic *fleutą.
From Old Norse fljóta, from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną.
From Old Norse fljúga, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-.
Doublet (showing a-mutation) of flug (“flight; cliff”), from Old Norse flog, flug (“flight; cliff; an illness of the head”), from Proto-Germanic *flugą.
From Old Norse floti, from Proto-Germanic *flutô (“raft”).
From Old Norse flog, flug (“flight; cliff; an illness of the head”), from to Proto-Germanic *flugą, related to *flugiz. Doublet (not showing a-mutation) of flog (“seizure”).

parole.significato: fly (the edge or half of the flag furthest from the flagpole)
parole.testo: From Old Norse flugr, from Proto-Germanic *flugiz.
From Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ (“flatfish”).

parole.significato: to move, to relocate (something or someone)
parole.testo: From Old Norse flytja, from Proto-Germanic *flutjaną.
From Old Norse flá, from Proto-Germanic *flahaną.
From Old Norse flœða, from Proto-Germanic *flōdijaną.
The noun sense is secondary to the verb sense, which is from Old Norse fletta, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną.
From Old Norse fló, from Proto-Germanic *flauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *plus- (“flea”).

From Old Norse flói (“marsh, swamp”), from Proto-Germanic *flōô (“expanse of water”), from Proto-Germanic *flōaną (“to flow, flood”). Cognate with Faroese flógvi (“gulf”) and Norwegian Bokmål floe (“marsh; water on marshland”)
From Old Norse flóki (“tuft of hair”), from Proto-Germanic *flukkōn-, *flukkan-, *fluksōn- (“down, flock”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“hair, fibres, tuft”).

From Old Norse flókinn. Past participle of a strong verb otherwise unattested in North Germanic: Proto-Germanic *flōkaną (“to beat”). The sense “matted, tangled” is derived from the practice of felt-making, one method of which was beating woolen cloth with a club, and from this is derived the sense
From Old Norse flóð, from Proto-Germanic *flōdą, a byform of *flōduz. Cognate with Norwegian, Swedish and Danish flod, English flood, Dutch vloed, German Flut.

parole.significato: a bad smell; stench, a malodorous smell
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse fnykr (“stench”), from Proto-Germanic *fnukjaz. The ultimate origin is obscure, but perhaps an expressive or imitative formation. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål fnugg, Danish fnug, Swedish fnugg.

From Old Norse fnœsa (“to sneeze, snort”), from Proto-Germanic *fnōsijaną (“to snort, puff”), from Proto-Indo-European *pnew- (“to breathe, pant”). Related to Old Norse fnasa, Old English fnēosan (“to sneeze”). More at English sneeze.
From Old Norse for-, from Proto-Germanic *fra-.
From Old Norse foringi, from Proto-Germanic *furaigangijô.
From Old Norse forn, from Proto-Germanic *fernaz.
From Old Norse forða, from Proto-Germanic *furþōną (“to advance”).
From Old Norse fram, from Proto-Germanic *fram.
From Old Norse framr, from Proto-Germanic *framaz.
From Old Norse fregna, from Proto-Germanic *frehnaną. Related to English frain.
From Old Norse frekr, from Proto-Germanic *frekaz.
From Old Norse frelsi, from Proto-Germanic *frijahalsaz (“freedom; free”).

parole.significato: to do, to commit (usually something bad, such as a crime)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fremja, from Proto-Germanic *framjaną.

parole.significato: frozen ground, ice on or in the ground
parole.testo: From Old Norse frør, frer (“frost”), from Proto-Germanic *fruzą, derived from *freusaną (“to freeze”), whence Icelandic frjósa.
From Old Norse freta, frata, from Proto-Germanic *fertaną, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-.
From older frerinn, from Old Norse frørinn (the original past participle of frjósa (“to freeze”), before -s- was generalized throughout the paradigm), from Proto-Germanic *fruzanaz.
From Old Norse friða, from Proto-Germanic *friþōną.

parole.significato: the lover of a married woman
parole.testo: From Old Norse friðill (“lover, gallant”), from Proto-Germanic *fridilaz. Compare frilla (“concubine, mistress, harlot”) (< Old Norse friðla).
From Old Norse friðr, from Proto-Germanic *friþuz.
From Old Norse frjáls, from Proto-Germanic *frijahalsaz.
From Old Norse frjó, from Proto-Germanic *fraiwą.
From Old Norse frjór (also frjár, frær), from Proto-Germanic *fraiwijaz.
From Old Norse frjósa, from Proto-Germanic *freusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *prews-, *prus-.
From Old Norse froskr, from Proto-Germanic *fruskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“jump, hop”). Sense #2 is semantic loan from German Frosch.
From Old Norse froða (which is also the source of English froth), from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ.
From Old Norse frum-, from Proto-Germanic *frumô and cognate to Old English forma.
From Old Norse frysta, from Proto-Germanic *frustijaną.
From Old Norse frá, from Proto-Germanic *fram.
From Old Norse frár, from Proto-Germanic *frawaz.
From Old Norse fræ, from Proto-Germanic *fraiwą, whence also the variant frjó.

parole.significato: kinsman, male relative (excluding brothers and direct ancestors or descendants), especially:
parole.testo: From Old Norse frændi, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz.
From Old Norse frǿða, from Proto-Germanic *frōdijaną (“to make wise, instruct”).

From Old Norse frœði, from Proto-Germanic *frōdį̄. By surface analysis, fróður (“knowledgeable”) + -i n (abstract noun suffix), or respectively + -i f (abstract noun suffix). Cognate to Faroese frøði, Swedish frode, and Middle High German vruote.
From Old Norse frétt, from Proto-Germanic *frihtiz.
From Old Norse frjá, from Proto-Germanic *frijōną, *frijaz, *frijô.
From Old Norse fríða, from Proto-Germanic *frīdijaną.
From Old Norse fríðr, from Proto-Germanic *frīdaz.
From Old Norse frón, Proto-Germanic *frōþną. The Old Norse word could be the source of the place Fron in Oppland, Norway.
From Old Norse fróðr, from Proto-Germanic *frōdaz.
From Old Norse frú, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.
From Old Norse fogl, fugl, from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz.

parole.significato: full (containing the maximum amount that is possible, allowed or expected)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fullr, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós.
From Old Norse fúrr, fýr, funi, from Proto-Germanic *fōr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥.
From Old Norse fura, from Proto-Germanic *furhō. Cognate with Danish fyr, Norwegian Nynorsk furu, Swedish fura, Dutch vuren, German Föhre, English fir.
From Old Norse fyl, from Proto-Germanic *fulją.
From Old Norse fylgð, from Proto-Germanic *fulgidō.
From Old Norse fylgja, from Proto-Germanic *fulgijaną.
From Old Norse fylla, from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną.
From Old Norse fylli, from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄.
From Old Norse fyrir (“before, for”), from Proto-Germanic *furi (“before, for”).
From Old Norse fyrirgefa, fyrgefa, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną. Cognate with Dutch vergeven, German vergeben, English forgive.
From Old Norse fyrstr, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz.
From Old Norse fá, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną. Doublet of fanga (“to capture, to seize”).
From Old Norse falki, from Proto-Germanic *falkô (“falcon”).

From Old Norse fáni, from Proto-Germanic *fanô. Compare the Latin pannus (“a cloth; a rag; a garment”), German Fahne (“the flag of a nation, organisation, etc; a banner”) from Middle High German vano / van, from Old High German fano (“a flag”), from the Germanic root *fanō (cloth, flag), from Proto-
From Old Norse fár, from Proto-Germanic *fawaz.
From Old Norse fár, from Proto-Germanic *fērą.
From Old Norse fægja, from Proto-Germanic *fēgijaną, related to *fagjaną (“to please”). See also fága (“to clean, polish”).

From Old Norse fæla (“to frighten away”), from Proto-Germanic *fēlijaną (“to frighten, terrify”), from *fēlaz (“frightening, terrifying”). Related to Norwegian fæl (“appalling”), Middle High German vālant (“fiend, demon”), Old Norse fála (“troll-woman”).
From Old Norse fǿrr, fœrr, from Proto-Germanic *fōriz (“able to go, passable”).

parole.significato: to move (a thing between places), to relocate
parole.testo: From Old Norse fœra, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną.
From Old Norse fœri, from Proto-Germanic *fōriją.

From Old Norse fœða (“to feed, to give birth”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-. Cognate to Faroese føða, Swedish föda, Norwegian and Danish føde, English feed, Dutch voeden.
From Old Norse fœða (“food”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-. Cognate to Faroese føði, Swedish föda, Danish føde, English food.
From Old Norse fé, from Proto-Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Indo-European *péḱu (“livestock, domestic animals”). Cognate with English fee.
From Old Norse fífl, from Proto-Germanic *fimfilaz. Cognate with Icelandic fimbul- (“mighty, great”) and Old English fifel (“monster, giant”).
From Old Norse folk, fólk, from Proto-Germanic *fulką.
From Old Norse fórn, from Proto-Germanic *fōrīniz, from *fōrijaną (whence Icelandic færa (“to move; to bring, offer, give”)).
From Old Norse fótr, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.
From Old Norse fǫlr, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz.
From Old Norse fǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *faznō (“snowdrift, snow-pile”), from Proto-Indo-European *pes- (“to blow, waft, drift”). Cognate with Faroese and Norwegian Nynorsk fonn.

parole.significato: a journey, a trip, a voyage
parole.testo: From Old Norse fǫr, from Proto-Germanic *farō.
From Old Norse fǫt (“clothes”), the plural of fat (“an article of clothing”), from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“idem”).
From Old Norse fǫðurligr, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz. Equivalent to faðir + -legur. Cognate with Danish faderlig, Swedish faderlig and English fatherly.
From Old Norse fúi, from Proto-Germanic *fūô, from Proto-Indo-European *puH-. Cognate with Faroese fúgvi.
From Old Norse fúll, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *puHlós, an adjectival derivation from Proto-Indo-European *puH- (“be rotten; putrid”).
From Old Norse fúna, from Proto-Germanic *fun- (“damp, mould, mildew”).
From Old Norse fúss, from Proto-Germanic *funsaz.
From Old Norse *fýla, from Proto-Germanic *fūlijaną. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz.

From Old Norse gagn (“benefit, advantage, use”), from Proto-Germanic *gagną, *gaganą (“gain, profit", literally "return”), from *gagana (“back, against, in return”), a reduplication of *ga- (“with, together”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”).
From Old Norse gala, from Proto-Germanic *galaną.
From Old Norse galdr, from Proto-Germanic *galdraz, related to gala (“archaic meaning; to chant spells, to sing spells”) from the Old English ġealdor.
Inherited from Old Norse galli, from Proto-Germanic *gallô.
From Old Norse gamall, from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz.
From Old Norse gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną. Cognates include Old English gamen (Modern English game).
From Old Norse ganga, from Proto-Germanic *ganganą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-.
From Old Norse gangr, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz.
From Old Norse garn, from Proto-Germanic *garną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰorn-, *ǵʰer- (“gut, intestine”).
From Old Norse garðr, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos < *gʰerdʰ-.

parole.significato: hole, perforation (an opening through a solid body)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą.
From Old Norse gata, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ.
From Old Norse gaukr, from Proto-Germanic *gaukaz.
From Old Norse *gauð (attested as Old Norse gauð f), from Proto-Germanic *gauþą (“barking, jest”).
Inherited from Old Norse gefa, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.
From Old Norse gegn, from Proto-Germanic *gagin. Compare German gegen; Old High German gagan.

parole.significato: to hold (a position), to serve (a purpose)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gegna, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną.
From Old Norse geil, from Proto-Germanic *gailō.
From Old Norse geirr, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰoysós (“throwing spear”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰey- (“to drive, move, fling”).
From Old Norse geiri, from Proto-Germanic *gaizô. Cognate with English gore.
From Old Norse geisa, from Proto-Germanic *gaaisōną, from *ga- + *aisōną.

parole.significato: beam, ray (of light, radio waves, showing control, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse geisli, from Proto-Germanic *gaisilaz (“stick, beam”).
From Old Norse geit, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from a substrate language.
From Old Norse gelda, from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną (“to castrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to cut”).
From Old Norse gengr, from Proto-Germanic *gangiz.
Inherited from Old Norse gør, from Proto-Germanic *garwiją or *gerwą.
Inherited from Old Norse gerr, gjǫrr, gǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *garwaz.
Inherited from Old Norse gerr, gjǫrr, gørr, from Proto-Germanic *garwiz, comparative of the adverb corresponding to ger (3).
From Old Norse gera, gøra, gørva, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną.

parole.significato: act, action (usually plural and more often as gjörð)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gørð, from Proto-Germanic *garwidō, related to the adjective *garwaz (“prepared, ready”). Compare the doublet gjörð.
From Old Norse geta (whence also English get), from Proto-Germanic *getaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“take, seize”). Compare Danish gide, Swedish gitta, English get.
From Old Norse geyma (“keep, watch”), from Proto-Germanic *gaumijaną; cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌿𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gaumjan).
From Old Norse geysa, from Proto-Germanic *gausijaną. Causative of gjósa (from *geusaną).
From Old Norse geð (“mind; mood; wits; senses”), from Proto-Germanic *gadją (“mind; courage”), of unknown origin.
From Old Norse gipt, from Proto-Germanic *giftiz.
From Old Norse gipta, from Proto-Germanic *giftijaną.
From Old Norse gil, from Proto-Germanic *gilją.
From Old Norse gimbr, gymbr, from Proto-Germanic *gimrī, cognate with Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira) & Latin hiems.
From Old Norse gjald, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).

From Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”). Cognates include English yield, German gelten, Dutch gelden, Swedish gälla, Norwegian gjelde, Faroese gjalda and Danish gælde.
From Old Norse gjalla, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną. Cognate with Swedish gälla, Danish gjalde, English yell, German gellen, Dutch gillen.
From Old Norse gjarn, from Proto-Germanic *gernaz.
From Old Norse gjósa, from Proto-Germanic *geusaną.

parole.significato: to spawn, to give birth to
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjóta, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną. Cognate with Swedish gjuta, Norwegian Bokmål and Nynorsk gyte, Danish gyde, Old English ġēotan, Dutch gieten.
From Old Norse gjǫf, from Proto-Germanic *gebō.
From Old Norse gjǫfull, from Proto-Germanic *gebulaz.
Inherited from Old Norse gørð, from Proto-Germanic *garwidō; a doublet of gerð. See also gera, gjöra.
Inherited from Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō, cognate with English girth.
From Old Norse glaðr, from Proto-Germanic *gladaz.
From Old Norse gler, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”).
From Old Norse *glenta, *gletta, from Proto-Germanic *glentaną (“to slide; glide”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰlend- (“to shine; sparkle; look”).
From Old Norse gleypa, from Proto-Germanic *glaupijaną.
Inherited from Old Norse gleðja, from Proto-Germanic *gladjaną.
From Old Norse glitra, from Proto-Germanic *glitrōną.
From Old Norse gljá, from Proto-Germanic *gliwēną, related to *glīwą (“gladness, joy”). Cognate with Faroese glíggja.

From Old Norse knúi, from Proto-Germanic *knukô.
From Old Norse knútr, from Proto-Germanic (compare *knuttan-, whence English knot).

parole.significato: shrine, typically in a home on farm; by extension a temple
parole.testo: From Old Norse hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą.

parole.significato: hole, cavity (indent into an object, e.g. the ground)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulą (“hole”).
From Old Norse hold, from Proto-Germanic *huldą, from Proto-Indo-European *kol-, *kwol-. Cognate with Danish huld, Norwegian Bokmål hold, and Swedish hull.
From Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs), Swedish huld.
From Old Norse hopp, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną.
From Old Norse hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną.
Inherited from Old Norse horr, from Proto-Germanic *hurhwą (“dirt, mucus”).
Inherited from Old Norse horr, from a nominalization of Proto-Germanic *hurhaz (“lean, thin”). Compare Latin gracilis (“lean”).
From Old Norse horfa (“to turn toward, face”), from Proto-Germanic *hwurbōną (“to turn, veer”).
From Old Norse hrafn (“a raven”), from the Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz, cognates with English raven. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-.
From Old Norse hrapa, from Proto-Germanic *hrapaną, *hrappa- (“fast”), from Proto-Indo-European *krb(ʰ)- (“quickly”). According to Kroonen, compare Dutch reppen.
From Old Norse hraukr (“pile”), from Proto-Germanic *hraukaz.
From Old Norse hraun, according to Pokorny, from the same source as Proto-Germanic *hraukaz (“haystack, pile”).

From Old Norse hraustr, from Proto-Germanic *hraustaz (“strong, active”). An older theory by Pokorny derives the Old Norse from Proto-Indo-European *kreu- (“to shake, wave around”), comparing Tocharian A kru (“reed”), Tocharian B kärwats, Lithuanian krutéti (“to move”) (though this is now considered
From Old Norse hraði, from Proto-Germanic *hrēdijaną, related to *hradjaną (“to loosen, set free”).
From Old Norse hraðr, from Proto-Germanic *hradaz.
From Old Norse hreinn, from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz.
From Old Norse hreinsa, from Proto-Germanic *hrainisōną.

parole.significato: to get, to receive (a prize or reward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse hreppa, from Proto-Germanic *hrappijaną.
From Old Norse hreppr (“municipal district”), from Proto-Germanic *hrampijaz, from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to shrink, contract, shrivel”). Cognate with Faroese reppur (“district”).
From Old Norse hreyfa, from Proto-Germanic *hraubijaną.
From Old Norse hrinda, from Proto-Germanic *hrindaną.
From Old Norse hringja, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną.
From Old Norse hringja, from Proto-Germanic *hringijǭ.
From Old Norse hringr, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz.

From Old Norse hrista, from Proto-Germanic *hristijaną (“to shake; to braid”). Older theories deriving the term from Proto-Indo-European *krisd- (“to move about, frolic”), and comparing with Sanskrit क्रीड् (krīḍ, “to play”), are semantically tenuous.

parole.significato: to cause to shudder [with dative ‘someone with a mind’ and við (+ dative) ‘at something’] (idiomatically translated as…
parole.testo: From Old Norse hrjósa, from Proto-Germanic *hreusaną.

parole.significato: to fly, be hurled (in a passive sense, as e.g. of objects flying around)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *hreutaną, perhaps related to Middle Low German rūzen. Probably from Proto-Indo-European *kreu-, as hrjóða, hrjósa and hrynja.
From Old Norse hrjúfr, from Proto-Germanic *hreubaz. Compare Old English hrēof, Old High German riob.
From Old Norse hrogn, from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”).
From Old Norse hroki, probably from hrokr (“heaped measure, pile”), from Proto-Germanic *hrukan-, *hraukaz.
From Old Norse hrollr (“shivering”), from Proto-Germanic *hruzlaz, related to the verb hrjósa (from Proto-Germanic *hreusaną).
From Old Norse hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą. Cognates with German Ross.
From Old Norse hrukka, from Proto-Germanic *hrunkǭ (“wrinkle, crease”).
From Old Norse hryggva, hryggja, from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną, *hriwwijaną.
From Old Norse hráki, from Proto-Germanic *hrēkô, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“to croak, crow”). Cognate with Old English hrǣċa (“retching, spittle”).
From Old Norse hrár, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz.

parole.significato: carcass; body of a dead animal or human
parole.testo: From Old Norse hræ, from Proto-Germanic *hraiwą.
From Old Norse hrækja (“to hawk, spit”), from Proto-Germanic *hrēkijaną. Cognate with Old English hrǣċan (“to clear one's throat, hawk, retch”).
From Old Norse hrǿra (“to stir, move”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną (“to stir”)
From Old Norse hræða, from Proto-Germanic *hrēdijaną, related to *hradjaną (“to loosen, set free”).

parole.significato: to enchant, to carry away, to move someone
parole.testo: From Old Norse hrífa (“to grip, snatch”), from Proto-Germanic *hrībaną (“to grip, snatch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ- (“to scratch”). Has become conflated with Proto-Germanic *rīfaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyp- (“to tear”), in each subsequent daughter language, cf. Old English gehr
From Old Norse hrím, from Proto-Germanic *hrīmą. Cognate with Danish rim, Swedish rim; also related to English rime, German Reim, Dutch rijm.
From Old Norse hrína, from Proto-Germanic *hrīnaną.
Inherited from Old Norse hrís, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą. Cognate with Faroese rís, Danish ris, Swedish ris, English rice, German Reis, Dutch rijs.
From Old Norse hróp, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaz. Cognate with Faroese róp, Danish råb, Swedish rop; compare also Old English hrōp, Old High German hruof.
From Old Norse hrópa, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną.
From Old Norse hrósa, from the same source as hróðr (“fame”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz.

parole.significato: to start, to jump (have a sudden reaction when startled)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hrøkkva, from Proto-Germanic *hrinkwaną.
From Old Norse hrǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *hraznō.
From Old Norse hrúga, from Proto-Germanic *hrūgǭ.
From Old Norse hrútr, from Proto-Germanic *hrūtaz, which is related to *herutaz (“stag”).
From Old Norse hunang, from Proto-Germanic *hunangą. Cognate with Faroese hunangur, Swedish honung, Danish honning.
From Old Norse hundrað, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).
From Old Norse hundr, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, from *ḱwṓ (“dog”).
Inherited from Old Norse hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hunhruz.

parole.significato: door (rigid movable pane designed to open and close a doorway)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hurð, from Proto-Germanic *hurdiz.
From Old Norse hvalr, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”).
From Old Norse hvar, from Proto-Germanic *hwar.
From Old Norse hvass, from Proto-Germanic *hwassaz.
From Old Norse hvatr, from Proto-Germanic *hwataz.

parole.significato: how (with reference to an adjective or an adverb)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hvat, originally the neuter form of *hver (from Proto-Germanic *hwaz), but conflated with hverr (whence Modern Icelandic hver). Corresponds to Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód, *kʷod. See hver.
Inherited from Old Norse hvé, inherited from Proto-Germanic *hwē.
From Old Norse hveiti, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz, from *hwītaz (“white”).
From Old Norse hvél (“wheel”), from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm. Compare Old Saxon hwiol, Old Frisian hwēl.

From Old Norse hverr (from Proto-Germanic *hwarjaz) and *hver (from Proto-Germanic *hwaz), which were conflated in late Old Norse. Most of the inflected forms of *hwaz have since become obsolete, and what remains in form is essentially the descendant of *hwarjaz, but with an extra form for the neute
From Old Norse hverr, from Proto-Germanic *hweraz.
From Old Norse hverfa, from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną.
Causative of hverfa (1). From Old Norse hverfa, from Proto-Germanic *hwarbijaną.
From Old Norse hvetja, from Proto-Germanic *hwatjaną.

parole.significato: gust, blast, burst (e.g. of wind, air, coughing)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hviða, from Proto-Germanic *hwiþō (“gust of wind”), from Proto-Germanic *hwi- (“to rush”), from Proto-Indo-European *kwei- (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”).
From Old Norse hválf, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbą.
From Old Norse hvelpr, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz, of uncertain origin.

From Old Norse hvína, from Proto-Germanic *hwīnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwey- (“to hiss, to whistle, to whisper”). Compare Faroese hvína, Swedish vina, Danish and Norwegian hvine, English whine.
From Old Norse hvítr, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos.
Inherited from Old Norse hvǫt, from Proto-Germanic *hwatō; compare Middle English whate.
From Old Norse hyggja, from Proto-Germanic *hugjaną.
From Old Norse hyggja, from Proto-Germanic *hugjǭ, related to hyggja (verb), hugur and hugi.
From Old Norse hylja, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną.

parole.significato: to attract the loyalty or favor of
parole.testo: From Old Norse hylla, from Proto-Germanic *hulþijaną, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (whence Icelandic hollur (“loyal”)). The sense “pay homage to” is due to influence from Danish hylde, Middle Low German hulden.
From Old Norse hylli, from Proto-Germanic *hulþį̄, from *hulþaz (“inclined, favourable (towards)”) + *-į̄ (“-th, -ness”). Equivalent to hollur (“beneficent, wholesome, loyal”) + -i.

parole.significato: a deeper section of a stream; a stream pool
parole.testo: From Old Norse hylr, from Proto-Germanic *hulhiz.

parole.significato: a carton in the shape of a tetrahedron or a triangular pyramid
parole.testo: From Old Norse hyrna, from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ. Related to horn (“an angle, a corner”).

parole.significato: rabble, beggars, white trash, low people
parole.testo: From Old Norse hyski (“household, family”) (also hýski), from Proto-Germanic *hīwiskiją (“household”).
From Old Norse háfr, from Proto-Germanic *hēbaz.
From Old Norse hálfdauðr, from Proto-Germanic *halbadaudaz. Equivalent to hálfur + dauður. Cognate with Danish halvdød, Swedish halvdöd, English halfdead and German halbtot.
From Old Norse halfr, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.
From Old Norse halmr, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz.
From Old Norse hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.
Inherited from Old Norse hár, hór, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz.
Inherited from Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą.
From Old Norse háss, from Proto-Germanic *haisaz.
From Old Norse háttr, from Proto-Germanic *hahtuz.
From Old Norse háð, from Proto-Germanic *hawiþą, related to *hauniz (“miserable”).
From Old Norse hæfr and hœfr, from Proto-Germanic *hēbijaz and *hōbijaz. Ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hōbiz.
From Old Norse hǿgri, comparative of hǿgr (“easy, convenient”), from Proto-Germanic *hōgiz. Cognates with the Danish højre and Swedish högra, höger.
From Old Norse hǿgr, from Proto-Germanic *hōgiz.
From Old Norse hæll, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz.
From Old Norse hœna, from Proto-Germanic *hōnijǭ, related to *hanjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”), *kana-.
From Old Norse hæra, from Proto-Germanic *hērijǭ, related to hár (“hair”). Compare Old English hǣre, Old High German hārra and hāra.
From Old Norse hæsi, from Proto-Germanic *haisį̄. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk hæse.
From Old Norse hætta, from Proto-Germanic *hanhtijǭ.
From Old Norse hætta, from Proto-Germanic *hanhtijaną. In the sense “stop” an unstressed prefix has likely been dropped, perhaps *ab-.

From Old Norse hæð, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō. Compare Norwegian høgd, Norwegian Nynorsk hædd, Faroese hædd, Swedish höjd, Dutch hoogte, Old High German hohida, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌹𐌸𐌰 (hauhiþa), English height.
From Old Norse héla, from Proto-Germanic *hehlǭ.
From Old Norse hér (“here”), from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r.

From Old Norse *héri, from Proto-Germanic *hezô, a variant of Proto-Germanic *hesô. Kroonen (2011) states that the Icelandic é in this word arose from the breaking of a short e into ja, the result of which underwent an r-umlaut to je, eventually merging with é /jɛː/ in Icelandic.
From Old Norse hófr, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Compare Danish and Swedish hov, English hoof, German Huf, Dutch hoef.

parole.significato: short, hollow cylinder or tube; socket (like the shaft socket on a speartip)
parole.testo: From Old Norse holkr, from Proto-Germanic *hulkaz (“cavity, hollow, recess”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”). Cognate with Swedish holk (compare Old Swedish holker), English holk.
From Old Norse hóll, from Proto-Germanic *huhalaz.
From Old Norse holmr, from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz.
From Old Norse hór, from Proto-Germanic *hōrą. Related to hóra (“whore”).

parole.significato: the lover of a married woman
parole.testo: From Old Norse hórr (“adulterer”), from Proto-Germanic *hōraz.
From Old Norse hóra, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”).
Inherited from Old Norse hósta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną.
From Old Norse hósti, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô.
From Old Norse hóta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtōną, from *hwōtō (“threat”).
From Old Norse hǫfuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”). More at English head.
From Old Norse hǫgg, from Proto-Germanic *hawwą, from the verb *hawwaną.
From Old Norse hǫggva, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną. Cognate with Danish hugge, Swedish hugga.
From Old Norse hǫll, from Proto-Germanic *hallō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, conceal, hide”). Cognate with English hall.
From Old Norse hǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.
Inherited from Old Norse hǫnk (compare haki (“something bent”)), related to Proto-Germanic *hakô (“hook”). Compare English hank.
From Old Norse hǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *hazwaz.
From Old Norse hǫrgr, from Proto-Germanic *harugaz.

From Old Norse húnn (“knob at the top of a mast-head”), from Proto-Germanic *hūnaz, *hūna(n)- (“top of a stick”).
From Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą.
Inherited from Old Norse húð, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz.

parole.significato: leech (blood-sucking annelid of the genus Hirudinea)
parole.testo: From Old Norse *iglr, from Proto-Germanic *egulaz (“leech”).
From Old Norse il, from Proto-Germanic *iljō.
From Old Norse inngangr, from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz.

Inherited from Old Norse iða, from Proto-Germanic *idōną (“to move about restlessly”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁i-t-eh₂-ie-, probably from *h₁éyti (“to go”). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål ide and Norwegian Nynorsk ide (“whirlpool”).
From Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. Compare Faroese javnur, Norwegian Bokmål jevn, Norwegian Nynorsk jamn, Swedish jämn, Danish jævn, English even, Dutch even, and effen, German eben.

parole.significato: a floating piece of ice; floe, iceberg
parole.testo: From Old Norse jaki, from Proto-Germanic *jekô, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yeg- or of later Finnic origin (compare Uralic *jäŋe 'ice').

parole.significato: peanut (a legume resembling a nut, the fruit of Arachis hypogaea)
parole.testo: From Old Norse jarðhnot, from Proto-Germanic *erþōhnuts, equivalent to jörð (“earth”) + hneta (“nut”).
From Old Norse jata, from Proto-Germanic *etǭ.
From Old Norse jaðarr, from Proto-Germanic *edaraz.

parole.significato: plant (living organism, usually not a tree)
parole.testo: From Old Norse urt, from Proto-Germanic *wurt- and possibly also *urtiz; both from Proto-Germanic *wrōts. Cognate with English wort.
From Old Norse já (“yes”), Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”).
From Old Norse járn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).
From Old Norse játa, from Proto-Germanic *jaatjaną.
From Old Norse jól, from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *yekə- (“joke, play”).
From Old Norse jór, from Proto-Germanic *ehwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos (“horse”).
From Old Norse jótar m pl, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz.
From Old Norse jóð, from a Proto-Germanic *euþą.
From Old Norse jǫkull, from Proto-Germanic *jekulaz. Diminutive of jaki (“a piece of ice, broken ice”).
From Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō.
From Old Norse jǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *jestuz.
From Old Norse oxi, uxi, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô, from Proto-Indo-European *uksḗn (“bull”) with the prefix jötun-.
From Old Norse júgr, from Proto-Germanic *eudarą, *ūdarą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ewHdʰ-r̥- (“udder”).
From Old Norse kafli, from Proto-Germanic *kablaz (“round piece of wood”).
From Old Norse kaldr (“cold”), from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz (“cold”), from Proto-Germanic *kalaną (“to be cold”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to be cold; to freeze”).
From Old Norse kalla, from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną.
From Old Norse kambr, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth (animate)”).
From Old Norse kanpr, kampr, from Proto-Germanic *kanipaz.
From Old Norse karmr, from Proto-Germanic *karmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, to wind”).

parole.significato: to throw, to fling, to hurl, to toss
parole.testo: From Old Norse kasta, from Proto-Germanic *kastōną. Cognate with Faroese and Swedish kasta, Norwegian and Danish kaste, and English cast.

parole.significato: cylinder (especially a wooden one); pin, roller
parole.testo: From Old Norse kefli, from Proto-Germanic *kablaz (“round piece of wood”); cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kjevle and Faroese kelvi, English cavel.
From Old Norse keipr, from Proto-Germanic *kaipaz.

parole.significato: a bog, a stagnant pit in a swampy ground
parole.testo: From Old Norse kelda (“a well, a spring”), from Proto-Germanic *kaldijǭ, cognate with Norwegian kjelde, Swedish källa, Danish kilde. Derived from *kaldaz (“cold”).
From Old Norse kemba, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną (from the Germanic root of kambur).
From Old Norse kenna, from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną.
From Old Norse ker, from Proto-Germanic *kazą. Doublet of kar, which was borrowed from Danish.
From Old Norse kerra, from Proto-Germanic *karzijaną. Compare Old English ċierran (“to turn”) (> English char, chore).

From Old Norse keyra, from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, whence also Danish køre (“to drive, travel”). No known direct correspondence in West or East Germanic, but perhaps cognate with English chare, German kehren, or with Serbo-Croatian журити (се)/žúriti (se) (“to hurry”).
From Old Norse kind, from Proto-Germanic *kinþiz, cognate with Latin gēns (“clan, tribe”). The sense of “sheep” is derived from the compound sauðkind, literally “sheep-kind”.
From Old Norse kinn, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu- (“cheek”). Compare Faroese and Norwegian kinn, Danish and Swedish kind, German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin.
From Old Norse kippa (“basket”), from Proto-Germanic *kippǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gey- (“to bend, twist, entwine”). Related to Dutch kiep, German Low German Kiepe, English kipe.
From Old Norse kitla, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną. More at kittle.
From Old Norse kið, from Proto-Germanic *kidją (“kid”).
From Old Norse kjarkr, from Proto-Germanic *kerkaz. Compare Norwegian kjerk (“vigour”), kjerkje (“stiffness of the neck”), kjerkje (“to bend the head back”).
From Old Norse kjarni, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂-n-on-, *ǵr̥h₂nóm, related to *kurną (“corn, grain”).
From Old Norse kjalki, from Proto-Germanic *kelkô.
From Old Norse kjósa, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-.
From Old Norse kjǫlr (“a keel”), from Proto-Germanic *keluz, cognates with the Faroese kjølur.
From Old Norse kjǫr, from Proto-Germanic *kuzą.
From Old Norse kjǫt, from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Cognate with Danish kød, Faroese kjøt, Norwegian Bokmål kjøtt, Norwegian Nynorsk kjøt, kjøtt, and Swedish kött.
From Old Norse klappa, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.
From Old Norse klefi, from Proto-Germanic *klebô (“chamber, cell”).
From Old Norse klemma, from or related to Proto-Germanic *klimbaną (“to clamp, clasp, climb onto”).
From Old Norse klettr, from Proto-Germanic *klintaz.

parole.significato: narrow pass on a cliff or mountainside
parole.testo: From Old Norse klif, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.
From Old Norse klifra, from Proto-Germanic *klibrōną.
From Old Norse kljúfa, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-.
Inherited from Old Norse klárr, from Proto-Germanic *klawaraz.
From Old Norse kláði, from Proto-Germanic *klawiþô, related to the verb *klawjaną (“to scratch”).
From Old Norse klífa, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną.
From Old Norse klina, from Proto-Germanic *klinaną (“to stick, smear”).
Inherited from Old Norse kló, from Proto-Germanic *klawō.
From Old Norse kløkkr, from Proto-Germanic *klinkwaz.

From Old Norse klǫpp (“a pierlike rock, stepping stone in a stream”), from Proto-Germanic *klampō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel (“to form into a ball”). See *klumpô (“clump, mass”), Middle High German klapf (“cliff top”), English clop (“rock, mound, hillock”).

parole.significato: to be able, can, (have knowledge to do): to know
parole.testo: From Old Norse kná, and its unattested infinitive *knega, from Proto-Germanic *knēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-. Cognate with English know.
Via Old Norse knár from Proto-Germanic *knawaz. Cognate with Crimean Gothic knau-.
Inherited from Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, originally from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.
From Old Norse knífr, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knīpaną (“to pinch”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneybʰ- (“to pinch”).
From Old Norse knǫrr (“merchant ship”), from Proto-Germanic *knarruz.
From Old Norse knýja, from Proto-Germanic *knūjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gnewH-.
From Old Norse koddi, from Proto-Germanic *kuddô. Compare Scots cod.
From Old Norse kofi, from Proto-Germanic *kubô.
Inherited from Old Norse kokkr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz.
From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷol-, from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”).

parole.significato: a rounded protrusion (such as a rounded mountaintop or a tussock)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kollr, from Proto-Germanic *kullaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“head”).
From Old Norse koma, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-.
From Old Norse kona (“woman, wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”).

parole.significato: kind, type (only used in the genitive, with an attributive adjective, determiner, etc., modifying a noun phrase)
parole.testo: From Old Norse -konar, genitive singular of Old Norse konr (“kind”), from Proto-Germanic *kuniz. Cognate with Old English cyne- (prefix).
From Old Norse konungdómr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz. Equivalent to konungur + -dómur. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål kongedømme, English kingdom and German Königtum.

From Old Norse konungríki, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to konungur (“king”) + ríki (“realm”). Compare Faroese kongaríki, Norwegian kongerike, Swedish kungarike, Danish kongerige, Dutch koninkrijk, German Königreich.
From Old Norse konungr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz.
From Old Norse korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
From Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz.
From Old Norse kostr, from Proto-Germanic *kustuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
From Old Norse krabbi, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô.
From Old Norse kraptr, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz.

parole.significato: collar (part of an upper garment fitting around the neck or a similar detachable item)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kragi, from Proto-Germanic *kragô (“throat”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ- (“throat, gullet”). More at craw.
From Old Norse krangr, possibly borrowed from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch, ultimatly from Proto-Germanic *krankaz.
From Old Norse krappr, from Proto-Germanic *krappaz.
From Old Norse krefja (“to demand”), from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną.
From Old Norse *krjósta, from Proto-Germanic *kreustaną (“to grind”).
From Old Norse kremja, from Proto-Germanic *krammijaną.
From Old Norse kreppa, from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną. Cognate to English crimp, via Middle English crempen, and to Dutch krimpen, via Middle Dutch crimpen.

parole.significato: to kneel down, to genuflect, to get down on one's knees
parole.testo: From Old Norse krjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“turn, wind”). Cognate with Norwegian krype, Swedish krypa, Danish krybe, English creep, Dutch kruipen.

From Old Norse krukka, from Proto-Germanic *krogu (“pot, pitcher”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics are problematic. Also compare Old Irish croicc
From Old Norse kryfja, from Proto-Germanic *krufjaną.
From Old Norse krá, kró, from Proto-Germanic *kranhō, of uncertain origin, found only in North Germanic; possibly related to *kringaną (“to turn”).

parole.significato: caw (representing the sound of a raven or crow)
parole.testo: From Old Norse krá, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *krēaną (“to crow”). Cognate with Faroese krá. Related to English crow (noun and verb).
From Old Norse krókr, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.
From Old Norse kundr, from Proto-Germanic *kundaz (“son; offspring”), from Proto-Germanic *kundaz (“born; akin”).

parole.significato: to know (by heart), know a skill
parole.testo: From Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.
From Old Norse kunnr, kuðr, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *kunnaną.
From Old Norse kunta, from Proto-Germanic *kuntǭ, cognate with English cunt.
From Old Norse kuti, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kutjaną (“to cut”). Cognate with dialectal Swedish kuta (“small knife”).
From Old Norse kveina, from Proto-Germanic *kwainōną.
From Old Norse kveisa, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰeydʰ- (“mud, filth”), see also Russian жи́дкий (žídkij), жи́жа (žíža).
From Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kweldą, *kwildiz.
From Old Norse kverk, from Proto-Germanic *kwerkō.
From Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-.

parole.significato: a greeting, the action of saying hello or goodbye
parole.testo: From Old Norse kveðja, from Proto-Germanic *kwadjaną. Cognate with Faroese kvøðja.
From Old Norse kvikna, from Proto-Germanic *kwiknaną.
From Old Norse kvikr, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz whence also English quick. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
From Old Norse kvæði, from Proto-Germanic *kwēþiją.
From Old Norse kví, from Proto-Germanic *kwījō (“enclosure, stable”).
From Old Norse kvísl, by dissimilation from Proto-Germanic *twīsilō.
From Old Norse kvǫl, from Proto-Germanic *kwalō.
From Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kweldą, *kwildiz.
From Old Norse kvern, from Proto-Germanic *kwernō.

From Old Norse kyn, from Proto-Germanic *kunją, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce”). Cognate with Faroese kyn, Danish køn, Norwegian kjønn, Swedish kön, English kin, Dutch kunne, as well as, more distantly, Latin genus (“kind, gender”) (whence English gender).
From Old Norse kynda, from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.
From Old Norse kynna, from Proto-Germanic *kunþijaną. Cognate with German künden, Dutch konden, English kithe.
From Old Norse kynni, from Proto-Germanic *kunþiją (“knowledge”).
From Old Norse kyrkja, kvirkja, from Proto-Germanic *kwirkijaną.
From Old Norse kyrr, kvirr, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz.
From Old Norse kyssa (“to kiss”), from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną.

From Old Norse kalfr (“calf”), from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷolbʰo- (“womb, animal young”). Compare Faroese kálvur, Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish kalv, Dutch kalf, German Kalb, English calf.
From Old Norse kátr, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz.
From Old Norse kœla, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną. Causative of kala.
From Old Norse kæna, kǿna, kani, from Proto-Germanic *kōnjǭ, a variant of *kanô (“boat”).
From Old Norse kœnn, from Proto-Germanic *kōniz. More at keen.
From Old Norse kæta, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtijaną.
From Old Norse kífa, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.
From Old Norse kíll, from Proto-Germanic *kiljǭ, ultimately related to *kīnaną (“to crack, split”).
From Old Norse kolfr, from Proto-Germanic *kulbaz.
From Old Norse kǫkkr, from Proto-Germanic *kankuz.

parole.significato: spider (any of various eight-legged, predatory arthropods, of the order Araneae, most of which spin webs to catch prey)
parole.testo: Altered from an earlier köngurófa, from Old Norse kǫngurváfa (whose first element is from Proto-Germanic *kangura-).

parole.significato: sickbed; a bed in which one lies bedridden
parole.testo: From Old Norse kǫr, from Proto-Germanic *karō (“concern, care”). See also Old Saxon cearu, Old English caru.

From Old Norse kúfa (“to heap, fill over the brim”), to the same root as Icelandic kúfur, Old Norse *kúfr (“elevation, heap, bulge, round top”), from Proto-Germanic *kūbaz, to Proto-Germanic *kubb-, from Proto-Indo-European *gup- (“round object, knoll”), from *gew- (“to bend, curve, arch, vault”).
