parole.significato: a bulge over the brim of a container which is more than full
parole.testo: From Old Norse *kúfr, from Proto-Germanic *kūbaz, related to Proto-Germanic *kubô. Cognate to Swedish kuv, Norwegian kuv. A Norse doublet appears to be kubbi.
From Old Norse kúla, from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ (“bump”).
From Old Norse kútr (“hide, bellows, a cask for liquor”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *keutaz, *kūtiz (“belly, intestines”).
From Old Norse kýr, from Proto-Germanic *kōz.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Norse laf, from Proto-Germanic *lappa-, of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). If so, doublet of lafa.
From Old Norse lafa, from Proto-Germanic *labēn- (“to dangle”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
From Old Norse lakr (“lacking, deficient”), from Proto-Germanic *lakaz (“slack, limp, loose, low”).
From Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz.

parole.significato: land, earth, ground (part of the Earth not under water)
parole.testo: From Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).
From Old Norse landamæri, second element from Proto-Germanic *mairiją (“mooring-post, post, boundary”), cognate with Old English mǣre (“boundary, border”).

parole.significato: to cause to want, to make feel like [with preceding accusative ‘someone’, along with í (+ accusative) ‘something’ or að…
parole.testo: From Old Norse langa (“to long for; desire”), from Proto-Germanic *langōną (“to desire; long for”), related to English long, German verlangen. More at long.

parole.significato: long (of distance or time or the length of an object)
parole.testo: From Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos.
From Old Norse latr, from Proto-Germanic *lataz.
From Old Norse lauf, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“peel, break off”).
From Old Norse laug, from Proto-Germanic *laugō.

From Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *launą, from a suffixed form of Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“catch, plunder, profit”). Cognate with Swedish lön, Dutch loon (Old Saxon lōn), German Lohn (Old High German lōn), Old English lean, Old Frisian lān, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌿𐌽 (laun). The Indo-European root is a
From Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *laugnō.
From Old Norse lausn, from Proto-Germanic *lausīniz.
From Old Norse lausung, from Proto-Germanic *lausungō.
From Old Norse lax, from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz.
From Old Norse laða, from Proto-Germanic *laþōną (“to invite”).
From Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną.
From Old Norse leggr, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)lak-. Cognates include the Swedish lägg and English leg.
From Old Norse leif, from Proto-Germanic *laibō. Cognate with English lave, Old High German leiba, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌱𐌰 (laiba).

parole.significato: to leave behind, especially to leave (food) uneaten
parole.testo: From Old Norse leifa, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną. Compare Faroese leiva, Danish levne, English leave.
From Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

From Old Norse leir (“clay, mud”), from Proto-Germanic *laiza- (“clay”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”). Compare dialectal English lair (“a bog, a mire”). Cf. Danish ler, Norwegian Nynorsk leire and Swedish lera.
From Old Norse leið, from Proto-Germanic *laidō.
From Old Norse leiða, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną, causative of *līþaną ( > Icelandic líða).

parole.significato: to cause to loathe, to cause to find disgusting
parole.testo: From Old Norse leiða, from Proto-Germanic *laiþijaną, from *laiþaz ( > Icelandic leiður).
From Old Norse leiðr, from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz. Compare German leid, where "einer Sache leid sein" (to be tired of something), still has the same meaning like the Icelandic cognate.
From Old Norse leka, from Proto-Germanic *lekaną.
From Old Norse lekr, from Proto-Germanic *lekaz. Compare Old English hlec, Dutch lek.
From Old Norse lemja, from Proto-Germanic *lamjaną.
From Old Norse lengd, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō.
From Old Norse lengja, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną. Related to lengd.
From Old Norse lepja, from Proto-Germanic *lapjaną (“to lick, lap; to scoop, ladle”); compare English lap.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Norse leppr (“lock of hair; rag”), from Proto-Germanic *lappaz, *lappô (“rag, cloth”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
From Old Norse lesa, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną.

parole.significato: to allow, to permit, to give permission for
parole.testo: From Old Norse leyfa, from Proto-Germanic *(uz)laubijaną.
From Old Norse leyfi, from Proto-Germanic *laubiją.
From Old Norse leyna, from Proto-Germanic *laugnijaną, whence also German leugnen.
From Old Norse leynd, from Proto-Germanic *laugnīþō, from Proto-Germanic *laugnijaną (“to conceal”), equivalent to leyna + -d. Cognate with Faroese loynd (“concealment, secret, secrecy”).

From Old Norse leysa, from Proto-Germanic *lausijaną. Cognate with Dutch lozen, English loose (from Old Norse lauss), obsolete English leese (from Old English līesan), German lösen; also Danish løse, Faroese loysa, Norwegian Bokmål løse/løyse, Norwegian nynorsk løyse/løysa and Swedish lösa.
From Old Norse leðja, from Proto-Germanic *ladjō-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂t- (“moist, wet”), and cognate with Welsh llaid (“mire”), Lithuanian latakas (“gutter”), Latin latex.
From Old Norse leðr, from Proto-Germanic *leþrą.

From Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”) (cognate with Faroese liva, Swedish leva, Danish and Norwegian leve, Dutch leven, German leben, English live).
From Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smudge, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”).
From Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.
From Old Norse limr, from Proto-Germanic *limuz.
From Old Norse lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindō.
From Old Norse lindi (“band, girdle, sash, belt”), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“flexible, ductile”).

From Old Norse linna, from Proto-Germanic *linnaną (“to move aside, swerve from, cease”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyh₂- (“to avoid, elude, decline, shrink away from, recede”). Cognate with English dialectal lin.
From Old Norse linnr, from Proto-Germanic *linþaz.
From Old Norse linr, from Proto-Germanic *linwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *leyh₂- (“to decrease, dwindle; lean, slim”). Cognate with Old High German len (“mild”).
From Old Norse list, from Proto-Germanic *listiz.
From Old Norse litr, from Proto-Germanic *wlitiz, *wlituz (“appearance, look, aspect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to see”).
From Old Norse lið, from Proto-Germanic *lidą (“flock, crowd, group”).
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.
Inherited from Old Norse ljá, léa, from Proto-Germanic *līhwaną.
From Old Norse lé ( < *léi, accusative ljá < léa, plural ljár < léar), from Proto-Germanic *lewô.
From Old Norse ljóma, from Proto-Germanic *leuhmô (“light, shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light; to shine”).
From Old Norse ljómi, from Proto-Germanic *leuhmô.
From Old Norse ljós, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsą.
From Old Norse ljóss, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz.
From Old Norse ljósta, from Proto-Germanic *leustaną.
From Old Norse ljótr, from Proto-Germanic *leutaz.
From Old Norse ljóð, from Proto-Germanic *leuþą.

parole.significato: to lie, to tell lies [about something]
parole.testo: From Old Norse ljúga (“to lie”), from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ-.

parole.significato: to finish, to end, to conclude (to bring to an end)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ljúka, lúka, from Proto-Germanic *leukaną, *lūkaną (“to shut, lock”). Of the two forms, ljúka and lúka, the latter is attested earlier.
From Old Norse logi, from Proto-Germanic *lugô. Cognate with Swedish låga (låge), Dutch laai.

From Old Norse logn lygn, from Proto-Germanic *lugnijaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright”), referring to shining water. Germanic cognates include English lown, Danish lyn (“lightning”), Swedish lugn (“calm water”).
From Old Norse lok, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“to close, shut, cover”).

parole.significato: a lock of hair, a curl
parole.testo: From Old Norse lokkr, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz.
From Old Norse loðinn, past participle of a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *leudaną. Compare Old English lēodan (“to grow”).
From Old Norse lund, from Proto-Germanic *lundō.

From Old Norse lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô (“lung”, literally “the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Faroese and Swedish lunga, Danish and Norwegian lunge, Dutch long, German Lunge, English lung.
From Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją.
From Old Norse lypta, from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną. More at lift.

From Old Norse lygn, from Proto-Germanic *lugnijaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright”), referring to shining water. Germanic cognates include English lown, Danish lyn (“lightning”), Swedish lugn (“calm water”).
From Old Norse lykill, from Proto-Germanic *lukilaz.
From Old Norse lyndi, from Proto-Germanic *lundiją. Cognate with Swedish lynne.
From Old Norse lyng, from Proto-Germanic *lingwą. Cognate with Faroese lyngur, Norwegian lyng, Danish lyng, Swedish ljung.
From Old Norse *lá, from Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to blame”).

parole.significato: the part of the sea near to the shore
parole.testo: From Old Norse lá, from Proto-Germanic *lahō, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus.
From Old Norse lágr, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz.
From Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.
From Old Norse láss, from Proto-Germanic *lamsaz.
From Old Norse lækna, from Proto-Germanic *lēkinōną.
From Old Norse lœkr, from Proto-Germanic *lōkiz.
From Old Norse lær, from Proto-Germanic *lahwaz.
From Old Norse læti, from Proto-Germanic *lētiją, from the root of láta (“to behave”).
From Old Norse létta, from Proto-Germanic *linhtijaną.
From Old Norse léttr, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.
From Old Norse líf, from Proto-Germanic *lībą.
Inherited from Old Norse lík, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

parole.significato: to please [with dative ‘experiencer’ and nominative ‘cause’] (idiomatically translated as “like”, with the dative objec…
parole.testo: From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną.
From Old Norse líkami, from Proto-Germanic *līkahamô.
Inherited from Old Norse líkr, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
From Old Norse lím, from Proto-Germanic *līmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH-, see also Latin limus. Cognate with Swedish lim, Norwegian Nynorsk lim and Danish lim.
From Old Norse líma, from Proto-Germanic *līmijaną.
From Old Norse lín, from Proto-Germanic *līną.
From Old Norse lína, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ.
From Old Norse líta, from Proto-Germanic *wlītaną.
From Old Norse lítill, from Proto-Germanic *lītilaz. Cognate with Faroese lítil, Danish liden, Norwegian liten, Swedish liten, Elfdalian litn.
From Old Norse líða, from Proto-Germanic *līþaną. The senses “suffer, tolerate” may be borrowed from Middle Low German, but derive from the same root in any case.
From Old Norse lófi, from Proto-Germanic *lōfô.
From Old Norse lómr, from Proto-Germanic *lōmaz.
From Old Norse lǫg, from Proto-Germanic *lagą; originally basically the same word as lag (“layer; song; …”), but in plural. Probably originally had the prefix *ga- in this sense.

parole.significato: drop of liquid (especially the last drop left in a bottle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse lǫgg, from Proto-Germanic *lawwō, from Proto-Indo-European *lowH-éh₂, from *lewH- (“to cut”) + *-éh₂. Cognate with Faroese løgg.
From Old Norse lǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *lagīniz.
From Old Norse lǫgr (“the sea; liquid”), from Proto-Germanic *laguz, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus. Cognate with the Old English lagu (“sea”), Latin lacus (“hollow, lake, pond”).
From Old Norse lǫm, from Proto-Germanic *lamō. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål lam (“strap hinge”).
From Old Norse lǫskr, from Proto-Germanic *laskwaz.
From Old Norse lǫstr, from the root of Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to blame, fault, reproach”), related to Old High German lastar (“vice”).
From Old Norse lauðr, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrą. More at lather.
From Old Norse lús, from Proto-Germanic *lūs.
From Old Norse lúta, from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną.
From Old Norse lýsa, from Proto-Germanic *liuhsijaną, derived from *leuhsaz (“light”, adjective) and/or *leuhsą (“light”, noun).
From Old Norse lýðr, from Proto-Germanic *liudiz.
From Old Norse magi, from Proto-Germanic *magô.
From Old Norse magr, from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.
From Old Norse maki, from Proto-Germanic *makô. Cognate with Danish mage, Swedish make, English match.
Inherited from Old Norse makki, from Proto-Germanic *mankô.
From Old Norse mala, from Proto-Germanic *malaną.

parole.significato: slightly rotten, beginning to taste of decay
parole.testo: From Old Norse *maltr, from Proto-Germanic *maltaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mold-o-s.
From Old Norse man, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *gamaną (with unstressed prefix *ga-).
Inherited from Old Norse marr, from Proto-Germanic *marhaz.
Inherited from Old Norse marr, from Proto-Germanic *mari.
From Old Norse mark, from Proto-Germanic *marką.

parole.significato: to mark an area, mark a boundary around something
parole.testo: From Old Norse marka, from Proto-Germanic *markōną.
From Old Norse masa, from Proto-Germanic *masōną. Cognate with English maze.

From Old Norse matr (“food”) from Proto-Germanic *matiz. Whence also Old English mēte (Middle English mēte from which English meat came); Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍄𐍃 (mats); Old High German maz, Swedish mat, Danish mad and Faroese matur.
From Old Norse maðkr, from Proto-Germanic *maþikô.

parole.significato: bedstraw, galium (plant of the genus Galium)
parole.testo: From Old Norse maðra, from Proto-Germanic *madarǭ; compare Swedish madra, Norwegian modre, English madder.

parole.significato: human being, person, humanity, mankind, man (generic)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse maðr, from Proto-Germanic *mann-, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mon-(u-) (“person”).

parole.significato: to be allowed, to be permitted, may
parole.testo: From Old Norse mega, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *magʰ-, *megʰ-.
From Old Norse megin, from Proto-Germanic *maginą.

parole.significato: to be able to, to be capable of

From Old Norse meitill, from Proto-Germanic *maitilaz. Cognate with Faroese meitil and Norwegian Nynorsk meitel.

parole.significato: to harm, hurt, wound, injure, damage
parole.testo: From Old Norse meiða, from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną or *maiþijaną.
From Old Norse melta, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną (“to dissolve, melt”). More at melt.

parole.significato: necklace, especially one with a pendant
parole.testo: From Old Norse men, from Proto-Germanic *manją. Compare Old English mene.

From Old Norse mergr, from Proto-Germanic *mazgaz < *mazgą, from Proto-Indo-European *mozgos, *mosgʰos. Compare Norwegian merg, marg, Swedish märg, Danish marv, Dutch merg, German Mark, English marrow.
From Old Norse merr, from Proto-Germanic *marhijō.
From Old Norse merja, from Proto-Germanic *marjaną.

From Old Norse merkja, from Proto-Germanic *markijaną.
From Old Norse meta, from Proto-Germanic *metaną.
From Old Norse meyrr, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz, perhaps related to Ancient Greek ἀμαυρός (amaurós) and Russian смурый (smuryj), хмурый (xmuryj).
From Old Norse meðal, from Proto-Germanic *midlą (“middle”). Compare Danish middel (“means, something used to cure”), which was instead probably borrowed through Low German.
From Old Norse mikill, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂-.
From Old Norse mildr, from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz, whence also English mild.
From Old Norse milti, from Proto-Germanic *miltiją.
From Old Norse minjar, from the plural of Proto-Germanic *minjō.

parole.significato: my, mine (used referring to someone/something masculine)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mínn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.

parole.significato: memory (the ability to remember things; not a particular recollection)
parole.testo: From Old Norse minni, from Proto-Germanic *gaminþiją.

parole.significato: to make smaller (in size or amount), reduce, lessen, decrease
parole.testo: From Old Norse minnka, minka, from Old Norse minni, minnr, or perhaps continuing a Proto-Germanic *minnikōną (“to make smaller, lessen, decrease”). Cognate with Norwegian minka (“to diminish, grow less”), Scots mink, munk (“to grow less, diminish”).

From Old Norse mis- (“mis-”), from Proto-Germanic *missa- (“wrongly, badly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mitto (“mutual, reciprocal”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to replace, switch, exchange, swap”).
From Old Norse missir (“loss”), from Proto-Germanic *miss- (“loss”).
From Old Norse miðja, Proto-Germanic *midjǭ (“centre”), *midją.

parole.significato: middle (referring to the middle of the thing modified by the adjective)
parole.testo: From Old Norse miðr, from Proto-Germanic *midjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo-.

From Old Norse mjǫlk, mjolk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, cognate with Danish mælk, Swedish mjölk, English milk. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-. Note the lack of i-mutation in the genitive (from *melukiz). Although the form would suggest a mutated **mýlkur, -jó- is not the original vow
From Old Norse mjǫk, from Proto-Germanic *mekō, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s; related to mikill (< *mikilaz, derived from a suffixed form of the same Indo-European word).
From Old Norse mjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *melwą.
From Old Norse mjǫll, from Proto-Germanic *mellō, related to *malaną (“to grind”).
From Old Norse mjǫðm (“hip”), from Proto-Germanic *medumō (“middle”).

parole.testo: From Old Norse mjǫðr, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“sweet drink”). Germanic cognates: Old Frisian mede, Middle Low German mēde, Dutch mede, Old High German mëtu (German Met) and Old English medu (whence mead). From Old Norse mold, from Proto-Germanic *muldō (“dirt, soil”).
From Old Norse morð, from Proto-Germanic *murþą.
From Old Norse mosi, from Proto-Germanic *musą. Cognate with Faroese mosi, Danish mose, English moss, German Moos, Dutch mos.
From Old Norse muna, from Proto-Germanic *munaną. Cognate with Faroese muna & English mind.
Inherited from Old Norse mund, from Proto-Germanic *mundō.
Related to Old Norse munda (“to aim, to strive”), Old High German muntar (“keen, eager”), from Proto-Germanic *mundraz (“alert”).

From Old Norse munda, from Proto-Germanic *mundōną. Compare with Faroese munda, Norwegian Bokmål munda (“to keep time”), Gothic mundon (“to draw attention”). Related to Ancient Greek μᾰνθᾰ́νω (mănthắnō, “to learn”), Sanskrit मन्धातर् (mandhātar, “pious, wise, person”), Proto-Slavic *mǫ́drъ (“wise”),
From Old Norse munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ment-.
From Old Norse munr, from Proto-Germanic *muniz.

parole.significato: cinquefoil, potentilla (plant of the genus Potentilla)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mura, from Proto-Germanic *murhǭ. Cognate with Faroese mura, Norwegian Nynorsk mure, Norwegian Bokmål mure.

parole.significato: to mildew, to mould, to grow mouldy, to grow muggy or musty, to moulder
parole.testo: From Old Norse mygla, from Proto-Germanic *muglōną, diminutive and denominative of *mukiz (“soft substance”) (compare Old Norse myki, mykr (“cow dung”)), from Proto-Indo-European *mewk- (“slick, soft”).
From Old Norse mygla, from Proto-Germanic *mugiljǭ. Compare Swedish mögel n, Norwegian Nynorsk mygle f, Trøndelag Norwegian møggel n and Gudbrandsdal Norwegian myngle f.

parole.significato: to grind, to pulverise, to crush
parole.testo: From Old Norse mylja, from Proto-Germanic *muljaną.
From Old Norse myrkr, from Proto-Germanic *merkuz. Cognate to English murk.
From Old Norse myrða, from Proto-Germanic *murþijaną.

parole.significato: one’s spouse’s brother or one’s sibling’s husband; brother-in-law
parole.testo: From Old Norse mágr (“relative by marriage”), from Proto-Germanic *mēgaz.
Inherited from Old Norse mál, from Proto-Germanic *maþlą.
Inherited from Old Norse mál, from Proto-Germanic *mēlą, whence also English meal. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European root *meh₁- (“to measure”).

From Old Norse mála, from Proto-Germanic *mēlōną, which could be related to *mailą (“spot, blemish, mark”). Cognate with Finnish maalata, Danish male, German malen (“to paint”) and Swedish måla from Middle Low German mâlen (“to draw, paint”).

parole.significato: metal (atomic element or material made of such atoms)
parole.testo: From Old Norse malmr, from Proto-Germanic *malmaz.
From Old Norse máni, from Proto-Germanic *mēnô, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also mánuður.

From Old Norse mánuðr, variant of mánaðr, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also máni. Cognate with Faroese mánaður, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål måned and Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk månad, English month, Old English mōnaþ
From Old Norse már, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz.
From Old Norse máttigr, from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz.
From older már (plural mávar), from Old Norse már, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz.

parole.significato: to speak, to say, to talk
parole.testo: From Old Norse mæla, from Proto-Germanic *maþlijaną.
From Old Norse mæla, from Proto-Germanic *mēlijaną.
From Old Norse mœna, from Proto-Germanic *mōnijaną- (“to tower”), from Proto-Indo-European *men-.
From Old Norse mær, from Proto-Germanic *mawī.
From Old Norse mærð, from Proto-Germanic *mēriþō. By surface analysis, -mar (“great”) + -ð f (abstract suffix).
From Old Norse mǿta, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną. Compare Norwegian møte, Danish møde, Swedish möta.
From Old Norse mætr, from Proto-Germanic *mētiz.
From Old Norse míga, from Proto-Germanic *mīganą, from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵʰ- (“to urinate”). Cognate with Old English mīgan; Latin mingo.
From Old Norse mót, from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, *gamōtą.
From Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
Inherited from Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, whence also English mood.

parole.significato: having a certain kind of mind or feeling
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, *gamōdaz.
From Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōþaz.
From Old Norse móðurlauss, from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlausaz. Equivalent to móðir + -laus. Cognate with German mutterlos and English motherless.
From Old Norse móðurligr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlīkaz. Equivalent to móðir + -legur. Cognate with Danish moderlig, Swedish moderlig and English motherly.
From Old Norse mǫgr, from Proto-Germanic *maguz.
From Old Norse mǫl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlō, derived from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”). Compare Proto-Germanic *muldō (“soil, dirt”).
From Old Norse mǫn, from Proto-Germanic *manō.
From Old Norse mǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *marhwaz.
Inherited from Old Norse mǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *markō.
From Old Norse mǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.
Inherited from Old Norse mús from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

Inherited from Old Norse mý, from Proto-Germanic *mugjǭ, *mują, from Proto-Indo-European *mu (“fly”), *mew-. Cognates with Norwegian mygg, Swedish mygga and mygg, Danish myg, Old English mycg (whence Middle English mygga, English midge); Old High German mucka (German Mücke (“mosquito”)); Latvian muš
From Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzī, from *meusą.
From Old Norse nafarr, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz.

From Old Norse naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą. Cognate with archaic English neat.
Inherited from Old Norse nauð, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, *nauþiz.
From Old Norse naðra, from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ. Cognate to Swedish nädra (“slowworm”).
From Old Norse naðr, from Proto-Germanic *nadraz. Cognate to Swedish näder (“slowworm”).
From Old Norse nef, from Proto-Germanic *nabją. Cognate with English neb.
From Old Norse nefna, nemna, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną. Cognate with Swedish nämna and English neven.
From Old Norse nei, from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né, *nē, *nēy (negative particle).
From Old Norse neinn, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz.
From Old Norse neita, from Proto-Germanic *niitjaną (“to say no”).

From Old Norse nema, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *nem-, *neme-.

parole.testo: From Old Norse nes (“headland”), from Proto-Germanic *nasją. Cognate with Old English næs (> English ness and naze); Swedish näs, German Nase. Compare also Latin nasus (“nose”) and Icelandic nös (“nostril”).
From Old Norse net, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).
From Old Norse neyða, from Proto-Germanic *naudijaną. Related to nauð, neyð.
From Old Norse neðan (“below, beneath”), from Proto-Germanic *niþanē (“below, beneath”).
From Old Norse gnit, from Proto-Germanic *hnits.
From Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include Danish and Swedish ned, English nether, Dutch neder, German nieder.

From Old Norse ná-, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz. Cognate with Old Saxon nāh, Dutch na, Old High German nāh (German nah and nahe); Swedish nära, Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐍈 (nēƕ); Old English nēah (English nigh).
From Old Norse náinn, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwinaz, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwaz (“nigh, near”).
From Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō.

From Old Norse nœgja, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgijaną.
From Old Norse næmr, from Proto-Germanic *nēmiz (“takeable, acceptable”).

From Old Norse né, from Proto-Germanic *nehw.

From Old Norse níundi, from Proto-Germanic *newundô.

Cognate with Old English nīþ, Old Saxon nīþ, Dutch nijd, Old High German nīd (> German Neid), Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐌹𐌸 (neiþ), Faroese níð, Danish nid and Swedish nid. From Old Norse gnógr, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz.

Inherited from Old Norse nátt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Old Norse nagl (masculine; plural negl), from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
From Old Norse nǫs, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s-.
From Old Norse nú, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”).
From Old Norse gnúa, from Proto-Germanic *ganū(w)aną, cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌰𐌽 (bnauan).
From Old Norse nú (“now”), from Proto-Germanic *nu.

From Old Norse nýra, from Proto-Germanic *neurô, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷʰrós.

From Old Norse oft (“often”), opt (“oft, often”), from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”).

From Old Norse okr, ókr, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz.
From Old Norse ǫlnbogi, alnbogi, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô. More at elbow.

From Old Norse opna, from Proto-Germanic *upanǭ.

From Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną. Doublet of yrkja.
From Old Norse ormr, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

From Old Norse otr, from Proto-Germanic *utraz, from Proto-Indo-European *udrós (“water-animal, otter”), from *wed- (“water”).
From Old Norse padda, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ (“toad”). Cognate with Faroese padda, Danish padde, Dutch pad, English pad.
From Old Norse panna, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ.
From Old Norse peningr, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Cognate with English penny.

From Old Norse plœgja, from Proto-Germanic *plōgijaną.
From Old Norse plógr, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz.
Frin Old Norse poki, from Proto-Germanic *puhô.

parole.significato: a knitting needle, a knitting pin
parole.testo: From Old Norse prjónn, from Proto-Germanic *preunaz. Cognate with Faroese prónur, Danish pryne, English preen, Scots preen. Compare also German Pfriem, Dutch priem from the variant *preumaz.
From Old Norse prófa, from Proto-Germanic *prōbōną, from Latin probō.
From Old Norse pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą.

From Old Norse púki, from Proto-Germanic *pūkô. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål puke, Danish pokker, and English puck.

From Old Norse rakr, from Proto-Germanic *rakaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-ó-s.

From Old Norse rangr, from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz, whence also English wrong.
From Old Norse rann, from Proto-Germanic *razną.

From Old Norse raun, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₁rou-neh₂-, which could be related to Ancient Greek ἔρομαι (éromai, “to ask”).

From Old Norse raust, ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to flow, boil, stream, move”). Related to Proto-Germanic *runsiz (“river”). Cognate with Danish røst, Faroese reyst, Norwegian Nynorsk røyst and Swedish röst.
From Old Norse rauðr, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz.
From Old Norse refsa, repsa, from Proto-Germanic *rafsijaną (“to punish, blame”).
From Old Norse regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną.
From Old Norse regnbogi (“rainbow”), from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô. Equivalent to regn (“rain”) + bogi (“bow”).
From Old Norse *regndropi, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to regn (“rain”) + dropi (“drop”).
From Old Norse regnvatn, from Proto-Germanic *regnawatōr. Equivalent to regn (“rain”) + vatn (“water”).
From Old Norse rein, reina, from Proto-Germanic *rainō. Cognate with English rean, German Rain.
From Old Norse reið, from Proto-Germanic *raidō.

Inherited from Old Norse reiði, vreiði, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþį̄, cognate with Swedish vrede, Danish vrede, Norwegian Nynorsk vreide. By surface analysis, reiður (“angry, wroth”) + -i f (abstract noun suffix).
From Old Norse reiðr, from older vreiðr, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz.
From Old Norse vreka (the v had disappeared already in later Old West Norse), from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną.

Probably from an Old Norse *renna (from Proto-Germanic *rannijǭ; see Etymology 2 below). See also Faroese renna (1), Norwegian Bokmål renne, Swedish ränna, Danish rende. Also related to Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐍉 (rinnō), Old High German rinna (both, from Proto-Germanic *rinnǭ).
From Old Norse renna (1), from earlier rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną; the alteration i > e is due to influence from the weak verb renna (2) (whence Icelandic renna (3)).

parole.significato: to cause (a liquid) to flow; to pour
parole.testo: From Old Norse renna (2), from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną. Causative of renna (2).
From Old Norse reykja, from Proto-Germanic *raukijaną.
From Old Norse reykr, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz.
From Old Norse reyta, from Proto-Germanic *rautjaną, related to *raupijaną (“to rip, pluck”).
From Old Norse reðr, from Proto-Germanic *ridrą, cognate with Faroese reður, Danish ræder. Compare also Icelandic hreðjar.
Inherited from Old Norse rif, from Proto-Germanic *ribją.

parole.significato: a tear, a rip, a rift, a rent
parole.testo: From Old Norse rífa (“to tear apart”), Proto-Germanic *rīfaną, from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to tear, cut”). Cognate with Scottish rive.
From Old Norse regna, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną (“to rain”), verbal form of *regną (“rain”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreǵʰ- (“to flow”).
From Old Norse rimma, related to ramr (“fierce, strong”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“overbearing, strong”).
From Old Norse risi, from Proto-Germanic *risiz.
From Old Norse rist, from Proto-Germanic *wristuz.
From Old Norse rit, from Proto-Germanic *writą.
From Old Norse ríta, rita, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey- (“to rip, tear”).
From Old Norse rið, from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną. Related to ríða.

parole.significato: the inner side (underside) of a roof (a traditional sloped roof with rafters)
parole.testo: From late Old Norse rjáfr, from older ráfr, from Proto-Germanic *rēfaz. Compare the alternative form ræfur (< Old Norse ræfr), which is due to a different leveling of the Germanic -az/-iz paradigm.
From Old Norse rjúmi, from Proto-Germanic *raumaz.

parole.significato: to break, interrupt (e.g. a connection, agreement, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rjúfa, from Proto-Germanic *reufaną.

parole.significato: to give off smoke or steam
parole.testo: From Old Norse rjúka, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. Related to reykur.

parole.significato: spinning wheel (device for spinning thread with a wheel and a spindle)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rokkr (“distaff”), from Proto-Germanic *rukkô.
From Old Norse roskinn (“ripe, mature”), from Proto-Germanic *wreskwaną (“to mature”).
From Old Norse rostungr (“walrus”), from Proto-Germanic *rustaz. Also see the genus Rosmarus.
From Old Norse rotna, from Proto-Germanic *rutāną.
From Old Norse rugga, from Proto-Germanic *rukkōną (“to rock”).
From Old Norse rykkja, from Proto-Germanic *rukkijaną (“to move, rock”).

From Old Norse ryðja, Proto-Germanic *rudjaną, a variant of Proto-Germanic *reudaną (“to clear”) (in Old Norse rjóða) and Proto-Germanic *rudōną (“to clear”) (cognates in German roden, rotten, reuten).

parole.significato: to wander, to ramble, to roam
parole.testo: From Old Norse ráfa, from Proto-Germanic *wabōną, *wabjaną (“to wander, sway”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move to and from, wander”).
From Old Norse rámr, from Proto-Germanic *rēmaz.
Inherited from Old Norse rás, from Proto-Germanic *rēsō.

From Old Norse ráða, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₁dʰ- (“reason, count”). Cognate with English read, Low German raden, Dutch raden, German raten, Swedish råda, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌳𐌰𐌽 (garēdan). The Indo-European root is also the source of Ancient Greek ἀριθμός (arithmós), Old I
From Old Norse rœgja, from Proto-Germanic *wrōgijaną. Related to Norwegian røyja, Swedish röja.

parole.significato: to attend to, to pursue, to perform
parole.testo: From Old Norse rœkja, from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną.
From Old Norse rœma, from Proto-Germanic *rōmijaną or Proto-Germanic *wrōmijaną, from the root of rómur (“voice”).
From Old Norse ræsa, from Proto-Germanic *rēsijaną.
From Old Norse ræsta, from Proto-Germanic *raskutjaną.
From Old Norse réttr (1), from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós.
From Old Norse rífa, from Proto-Germanic *rīfaną. Cognate with the English rive, Danish rive, Norwegian rive.
From Old Norse ríki, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją, from Proto-Germanic *rīks, an early borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs.
From Old Norse ríkja (whence also > Middle English riken (“to reign”)), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaną.
From Old Norse ríkr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, a derivative of *rīks (“king, ruler”), itself a borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs.
From Old Norse rísa, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey-.
From Old Norse ríða (“to ride”), from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *reydʰ-, cognate with English ride.
From Old Norse vríða, from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną.
Inherited from Old Norse ró (whence also Danish ro), from Proto-Germanic *rōō.

parole.significato: to row, to propel a vessel with oars
parole.testo: From Old Norse róa, from Proto-Germanic *rōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁-.

From Old Norse rót (“root”), from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”); compare with English wort and the Latin rādīx (“root”). Cognate with the Faroese rót; Old English rōt (whence the Middle English word root (“the underground part of a plant”) came, whence the English
From Old Norse róðr, from Proto-Germanic *rōþrą.
From Old Norse rǫdd (“voice, speech”), from Proto-Germanic *razdō (“voice, speech”). More at reard.
From Old Norse rǫk, from Proto-Germanic *rakō.
From Old Norse røkkr, røkr, from Proto-Germanic *rekwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁régʷos.

parole.significato: quick, prompt, quick to do/finish (especially what one is asked)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫskr, from Proto-Germanic *wraskwra-, from Proto-Indo-European *wrésgʷ-e-.
From Old Norse rǫð, from Proto-Germanic *radō.
From Old Norse rugr, from Proto-Germanic *rugiz. Cognate with Faroese rugur, Danish rug, Swedish råg, Dutch rogge, German Roggen, and English rye.
From Old Norse rúm, from Proto-Germanic *rūmą, from Proto-Indo-European *rewh₁-.
From Old Norse rúmr, from Proto-Germanic *rūmaz.
From Old Norse rýja, from Proto-Germanic *rūjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH- (whence also Latin ruō, Lithuanian ráuti).
From Old Norse rýma, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną.
From Old Norse rýna, from Proto-Germanic *rūnijaną. Compare Icelandic rún, Old English rēonian.
From Old Norse safi, from Proto-Germanic *safô (“sap, berry juice”), from Proto-Indo-European *sap- (“to taste, perceive”). Compare Old English sāfor (“drool, slobber”).
From safna, from Old Norse safna, a by-form of samna (“to collect, assemble”), from Proto-Germanic *samnōną (“to gather, collect”). More at sam.
From Old Norse samna, safna, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną, *samanōną.

From Old Norse saga, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ. Cognate with Old English sagu (English saw); Old Frisian sege; Old High German saga (German Sage); Old Danish saghæ, Old Swedish sagha, Faroese søga, Nynorsk soge, Jutlandic save (“a narrative, a narration, a tale, a report”), Swedish saga. Perhaps rel
From Old Norse saka, from Proto-Germanic *sakōną.
From Old Norse sala, from Proto-Germanic *salō.
From Old Norse salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l, *sáls.
From Old Norse saltr, from Proto-Germanic *saltaz.

From Old Norse samband, from Proto-Germanic *sambandą, from Proto-Indo-European *som-bʰondʰ-ó-m, from *som- (“together”) + *bʰendʰ- (“to bind”) + *-ós. Equivalent to sam- (“together”) + band (“connection, binding”). Cognate with Sanskrit सम्बन्ध m (sambandhá, “connection, binding”), Ossetian ӕмбонд
From Old Norse samr, from Proto-Germanic *samaz.
From Old Norse samvist, from Proto-Germanic *samaz + *wistiz, corresponding to sam- + vist.
From Old Norse sandr, from Proto-Germanic *samdaz.
From Old Norse sannsǫgull, from Proto-Germanic *sanþasagulaz. Cognate with Old English sōþsagol and Norwegian Nynorsk sannsogol. Equivalent to sannur + -sögull.
From Old Norse sannr, saðr, from Proto-Germanic *sanþaz.
From Old Norse saurr, from Proto-Germanic *sauraz.
From Old Norse sjaután, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun.
From Old Norse segja, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to say”).
From Old Norse segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą.

From Old Norse seinn (whence also Swedish sen), from Proto-Germanic *sainaz, *sainijaz, perhaps related to *sīþuz (“late”), which may imply derivation from some reflex of Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). See also Lithuanian at-sainùs (“careless”).
From Old Norse seiðr, from Proto-Germanic *saidaz, from Proto-Indo-European *soytós.

From Old Norse sekkr, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic. Cognate with Dutch zak, German Sack, Swedish säck, Hebrew שַׂק (śaq, “sack, sackcloth”), Akkadian 𒆭𒊓 (saqqu).
From Old Norse sekr, from Proto-Germanic *sakjaz.
From Old Norse selja (“sell”), from Proto-Germanic *saljaną.
From Old Norse selja (whence also Swedish sälg), from Proto-Germanic *salhijǭ, a variant of *salhô (whence English sallow).
Inherited from Old Norse selr, from Proto-Germanic *selhaz. Cognate with English seal.
From Old Norse sem (“as, like”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *samaz (“same, alike”).
From Old Norse semja, from Proto-Germanic *samjaną.
From Old Norse senda, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną.

parole.significato: to fuck, to have (penetrative) sex with
parole.testo: From Old Norse serða, from Proto-Germanic *serþaną.
From Old Norse sess, from Proto-Germanic *sessaz (“seat”). Cognate with Old English sess (“seat”).
From Old Norse set, from Proto-Germanic *setą. Compare the English seat.
From Old Norse setja, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną.
From Old Norse sex, from Proto-Germanic *sehs. Cognates include Faroese seks and Danish seks.
From Old Norse sextán, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun.

parole.significato: to fill, to satiate, to sate
parole.testo: From Old Norse seðja, from Proto-Germanic *sadjaną. Compare the Latin satiō (“I satisfy”).

parole.significato: oneself (and also depending on context himself, herself, itself and themselves)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse sik, from Proto-Germanic *sik.
From Old Norse sigla, from Proto-Germanic *siglijaną.
From Old Norse sigra, from Proto-Germanic *sigizōną.
From Old Norse sigr (“victory”) (whence also Danish sejr, Swedish seger), from Proto-Germanic *segaz. Cognate with Old English siġe, German Sieg (“victory”), and Yiddish זיג (zig, “victory”).
From Old Norse sigð, from Proto-Germanic *sigiþō.

parole.significato: third-person reflexive possessive determiner: his (own), her (own), its (own), their (own)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sínn, sinn from Proto-Germanic *sīnaz.

From Old Norse sinn, from Proto-Germanic *sinþaz (“journey, way; time, occurrence”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”). Cognate with Faroese sinn, Danish sinde, Swedish sin (in någonsin (“ever; at any time”)); more distantly Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐌽𐌸𐍃 (sinþs), Old High German sind.
From Old Norse sitja, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).
From Old Norse siða, from Proto-Germanic *sidōną.

From Old Norse siðr (“a custom, a habit; conduct, morality, religion”), from Proto-Germanic *siduz, from Proto-Indo-European *swe-dh-. Cognate to Old English sidu (“a custom; a manner; a rite; purity”), Old High German situ (“a custom, a habit”) (whence the German Sitte), Faroese siður (“a tradition

parole.significato: to see, to sense or perceive with one's eyes
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse sjá, séa, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”).
From Old Norse sjálfr, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”).
From Old Norse sjón, from Proto-Germanic *siuniz. Doublet of sýn.
From Old Norse sær, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz.
From Old Norse sjóða, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.
From Old Norse sjóðr, from Proto-Germanic *seudaz, cognate with Lithuanian siūdas. Originally a nominalized past participle of Proto-Indo-European *syewH- (“to sew”) (Proto-Germanic *siwjaną).
From Old Norse sjau, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
From older sétti, from Old Norse sétti, from Proto-Germanic *sehtô.
From Old Norse sjaundi, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô.
From Old Norse súga, from Proto-Germanic *sūganą, from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-.
From Old Norse sjúkr, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz.
From Old Norse skafa, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”).
From Old Norse skafl, from Proto-Germanic *skabalō-. Compare Norwegian skavl, Faroese skalvur.
From Old Norse skapt, from Proto-Germanic *skaftaz. Cognate with English shaft, German Schaft, Danish skaft.
From Old Norse skagi, from Proto-Germanic *skagô.

From Old Norse skaka (“to shake”), from Proto-Germanic *skakaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kek- (“to shake, stir”). Compare Norwegian skake, Swedish skaka, Danish skage, Low German schaken, English shake.
From Old Norse skakkr, from Proto-Germanic *skankaz.
From Old Norse skalli (“a bald head; skull”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *skaljō (“shell, husk”).
From Old Norse skamr, skammr, from Proto-Germanic *skammaz, cognate with Old English sceam, scamm and Old High German scam.
From Old Norse skap, from Proto-Germanic *skapą (“shape, nature, condition”).
From Old Norse skarfr, from Proto-Germanic *skarf-, *skarb-, *skraf-, of imitative origin.
From Old Norse skarpr, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
From Old Norse skarð, from Proto-Germanic *skardą.
From Old Norse skatta, from Proto-Germanic *skattōną.
From Old Norse skattr, from Proto-Germanic *skattaz.
From Old Norse skaða, from Proto-Germanic *skaþōną (“to injure”). Cognate with English scathe and German schaden.
From Old Norse skaði, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keh₁t- (“damage, harm”).
From Old Norse skegg, from Proto-Germanic *skagją, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kek-, *(s)keg- (“to jump, skip, move, hurry”).
From Old Norse skeina, from Proto-Germanic *skainō (“skin wound, scratch”).
Inherited from Old Norse skeið (“a ship, a sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *skaiþiz.
Inherited from Old Norse skeið (“race; race course; piece of way; space of time”), from Proto-Germanic *skaiþaną (“to separate”), ultimately from the same origin as the "spoon" sense of Etymology 1.
From Old Norse skeiða, from Proto-Germanic *skaiþōną.
From Old Norse skekkja (“to skew; displace”), from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną. Doublet of skenkja. Related to Icelandic skakkur (“skewed”).
From Old Norse skel, from Proto-Germanic *skaljō.

parole.significato: an instance of something being damaged or spoiled; damage, spoilage
parole.testo: From Old Norse skemmd (“shame, disgrace”), from Proto-Germanic *skammiþō.

parole.significato: to pour, to pour out (portions, e.g. of a drink)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skenkja, from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną. Doublet of skekkja.
From Old Norse skepna, from Proto-Germanic *skapnijǭ, from the past participle of *skapjaną.
From Old Norse sker, from Proto-Germanic *skarją. Compare Middle Low German schere, German Schere (“gap”), Old English scorian (“to project; jut”).
From Old Norse skera, from Proto-Germanic *skeraną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
From Old Norse skeyta, from Proto-Germanic *skautijaną.
From Old Norse skikkja, from Proto-Germanic *skikkijǭ, from *skekkô (“mantle, cape”). Cognate with Old High German skekko (“mantle”), Old English sċiċċels (“cloak, cape”).
From Old Norse skilja, from Proto-Germanic *skiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH-.
From Old Norse skinn, from Proto-Germanic *skinþą.
From Old Norse skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą.
From Old Norse skipa from Proto-Germanic *skipōną.

parole.significato: to divide, to partition, to cleave
parole.testo: From Old Norse skipta, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną.

parole.significato: the membrane between the shell and the egg white
parole.testo: From Old Norse skjall, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to divide”) or *(s)kel- (“to cover”). See also Proto-Germanic *skal- (“testicles”).
From Old Norse skjalfa, from Proto-Germanic *skelbaną.

parole.significato: a window screen made of an animal membrane used instead of glass
parole.testo: From Old Norse skjár, from an earlier *ské (<*skéi, similar in composition to lé, klé), whence also Faroese skíggi. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skĭa-, *skiō-, related to *skīnaną (“to appear, shine”).

From Old Norse skjól, from Proto-Germanic *skeulą, according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split”). Or, from *(s)kewH- (“to cover”), related to Proto-Germanic *hūdijaną (“to conceal”), Sanskrit स्कुनाति (skunā́ti, “he covers”).
From Old Norse skjóla, from Proto-Germanic *skeulǭ, related to skjól (“shelter”).

From Old Norse skjór, from Proto-Germanic *skaiwarō-, of uncertain ultimate origin. Possibly Proto-Indo-European *kik- (Lithuanian kḗkštas, Greek κίσσα (kíssa), Sanskrit किकिदीवि (kikidīvί, “blue jay”)).
From Old Norse skjóta, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd-.
From Old Norse skjótr, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaz.

From Old Norse skjǫldr, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keit-, *(s)keid-, *kheit- (“shield, cover”). Compare Faroese skjøldur, Danish and Norwegian skjold, Swedish sköld.
Inherited from Old Norse skǫr, from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“division, portion”).
From Old Norse skor, from Proto-Germanic *skurǭ (“incision; tear; rift”), which is related to *skeraną (“to cut, shear”).
From Old Norse skortr, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål skort, Old English sċeort, sċeort, Old Frisian *skort, and Old High German scurt or scurz.
From Old Norse skot, from Proto-Germanic *skutą.
From Old Norse skopt (“lock of hair, hair from the head”) (whence also Nynorsk skoft (“tail [of birds]”)), from Proto-Germanic *skuftą.

parole.significato: to view, to observe, to watch, to check out
parole.testo: From Old Norse skoða, related to Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look”) and *skauniz (“shining”), all from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”).
From Old Norse skratti, from Proto-Germanic *skrattuz.
From Old Norse skreppa (“to slip”), Proto-Germanic *skrimpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerbʰ- (“to turn, curve”), an extension of *(s)ker- (“turn”).

From Old Norse skrifa, from Proto-Germanic *skrībaną, a late borrowing from Latin scrībō (“write”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ-. Compare Faroese skriva, Danish skrive, West Frisian skriuwe, Low German schrieven, Dutch schrijven, German schreiben, Swedish skriva.
From Old Norse skriða, from Proto-Germanic *skrīþaną (“to glide, crawl”). Borrowed into English as scree.
Inherited from Old Norse skrá, from Proto-Germanic *skrahō.
From an unattested Old Norse skríkja, from Proto-Germanic *skrīkijaną (“to cry out”).

parole.significato: to slither (as a snake, as a ship over water, on snowshoes over snow)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skríða, from Proto-Germanic *skrīþaną.

parole.significato: to decorate, dress in fine robes, jewels, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Norse skrýða (literally “to shroud”), from Proto-Germanic *skrūdijaną.
From Old Norse skuggi, from Proto-Germanic *skuwwô (“shadow, reflection”).
From Old Norse skuld, from Proto-Germanic *skuldiz.
From Old Norse skulu, skolu, from Proto-Germanic *skulaną.
From Old Norse skurðr, from Proto-Germanic *skurdiz.
From Old Norse skutr, from Proto-Germanic *skutiz.
From Old Norse skál, from Proto-Germanic *skēlō.
From Old Norse skǽrr, from Proto-Germanic *skairiz. Related to skír and skína.
From Old Norse skína, from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną.
From Old Norse skírr, from Proto-Germanic *skīriz or *skīrijaz.
From Old Norse skíta, from Proto-Germanic *skītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd-, *sḱeyd- (“to cut off”).

From Old Norse skǫmm, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European. Compare Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish skam, German Scham, English shame, Dutch schaamte.
From Old Norse ský, from Proto-Germanic *skiwją (“cloud, cloud cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”).

parole.testo: From Old Norse skýla, from Proto-Germanic *skiulijaną. Cognate with Swedish skyla, Caithness Norn skỳl.
From Old Norse skýli, from Proto-Germanic *skiuliją.

parole.significato: A beat, stroke, blow (an act of hitting, beating, striking).

From Old Norse slakr, from Proto-Germanic *slakaz, cognate with English slack.
From Old Norse sleggja, from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.
From Old Norse sleikja, from Proto-Germanic *laigōną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ-.
From Old Norse sleipr, from Proto-Germanic *slaipaz.

From Old Norse sleði, from Proto-Germanic *slidô, related to *slīdaną, whence English slide.

From Old Norse slá (“bar; crossbeam; bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *slahō.

parole.testo: From Old Norse slátr, from Proto-Germanic *slahtrą, from *slahaną (“to hit, strike”) (whence Icelandic slá).
From Old Norse slœgja, from Proto-Germanic *slōgijōną.

From Old Norse sløkkva, from Proto-Germanic *slakwjaną. Probably not related to English slake, which originally meant “to weaken”.

From Old Norse smiðja, from Proto-Germanic *smiþjǭ.

parole.testo: From Old Norse smiðr, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz. Compare Norwegian and Swedish smed, German Schmied, Dutch smid, English smith.
From Old Norse smjǫr, smør, from Proto-Germanic *smerwą. Cognate with Swedish smör, Faroese, Norwegian and Danish smør.

parole.significato: to creep (through an entrance), to slip in
parole.testo: From Old Norse smjúga, from Proto-Germanic *smeuganą.
From Old Norse smyrill, from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz.

parole.significato: to butter; to cover (e.g. a slice of bread) with butter or another spread
parole.testo: From Old Norse smyrva, smyrja, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną.
From Old Norse smyrsl, from Proto-Germanic *smirwislą.
From Old Norse smár, from Proto-Germanic *smēhaz.
From Old Norse smíða, perhaps originally a strong verb, from Proto-Germanic *smīþaną; else derived from smíð, smíði.

From Old Norse snagi (“clothes peg”), reflecting Proto-Germanic *snagô, perhaps the same or a related n-stem noun *snag(g)- ~ *snakk- whence *snēkô (“snake”), according to Kroonen the source of *snakaną (“to crawl, creep”) rather than the reverse as usually assumed.
From Old Norse snara, from Proto-Germanic *snarhǭ (“sling”), synchronically analyzed as a deverbal from snara (“to snare, lasso”), see lemma below.
From Old Norse snarpr, from Proto-Germanic *sner-.

parole.significato: slice; a piece that has been cut off something
parole.testo: From Old Norse sneið (i-stem), from Proto-Germanic *snaidiz. Cognate with Old English snǣd (“morsel, bit”) and Old Frisian snēde (“slice”).

From Old Norse sneiða, from Proto-Germanic *snaidijaną (“to cut, slice”), causative of Proto-Germanic *snīþaną (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *sneyt- (“to cut”). Cognate with Old English snǣdan (“to cut into slices”).
From Old Norse snemma, snimma, from Proto-Germanic *sneumô. Cognate with Faroese snimma.
From Old Norse snepill (“snip, flap”), from Proto-Germanic *snipilaz (“idem”).
From Old Norse snigill, from Proto-Germanic *snigilaz.

From Old Norse snákr (“snake”) (only in poetry) and synonymous snókr, from Proto-Germanic *snakô; cognates include Danish snog (“a snake”), Swedish snok, English snake.
From Old Norse snœri, related to Proto-Germanic *nēaną (“to sew”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin”).
From Old Norse sníða, from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sneyt- (“to cut”). Compare Swedish snida, Dutch snijden, German schneiden, dialectal English snithe.
From Old Norse snøggr, snǫggr, related to Proto-Germanic *snauþuz. Cognate with Swedish snygg.
From Old Norse snúa, from Proto-Germanic *snōwaną, *snewaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sneh₁- (“to wind; twist; braid; plait”).
From Old Norse snýta, from Proto-Germanic *snūtijaną.

From Old Norse sonr, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús.
From Old Norse sorg, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”).
From Old Norse soð, from Proto-Germanic *sudą, from the root of sjóða (“to boil”).
From Old Norse spara, from Proto-Germanic *sparāną, from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to be productive; earn”). Cognate with Danish spare, English spare and German sparen.
From Old Norse sparka, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *spurnaną (“to trample, kick”). Compare Swedish sparka.
From Old Norse spaði, from Proto-Germanic *spadô.
From Old Norse speni, from Proto-Germanic *spenô. More at English spean.
From Old Norse spenna, from Proto-Germanic *spannijaną. Cognate with Faroese spenna, Norwegian Nynorsk spenna, Swedish spänna, Danish spænde.

parole.significato: to corrupt, to contaminate, to mar
parole.testo: From Old Norse spilla, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną.

From Old Norse spinna, from Proto-Germanic *spinnaną. Cognate with Faroese spinna, Swedish spinna, Norwegian Bokmål spinne, Norwegian Nynorsk spinna, spinne, Danish spinde, English spin, Dutch spinnen, German spinnen, German Low German spinnen.
From Old Norse spjald, speld, from Proto-Germanic *speldą.

parole.significato: to crack, break, split open, burst
parole.testo: From Old Norse springa, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sprenǵʰ-.

From Old Norse sprækr (“nimble, lively”) from Proto-Germanic *sprēkijaz (“lively”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)preg- (“to strew, jerk, sprinkle, scatter”). Cognates include English spry, sprey, Norwegian sprek (“lively, healthy”), Swedish dialectal sprygg (“brisk, very active, skittish”).
From Old Norse spyrja, from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną. Cognate with Old English spyrian, German spüren, Danish spørge.
From Old Norse spyrna, from Proto-Germanic *spurnijaną (“to kick”). Compare Icelandic sparka.

From Old Norse spǫng, from Proto-Germanic *spangō (“brooch, clasp”).
From Old Norse spǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *spannō.

From Old Norse stakkr (“a short garment; doublet”), from Proto-Germanic *stakkaz (“a short jacket”), from *stakkaz (“short”).

From Old Norse stara, from Proto-Germanic *starjaną.

From Old Norse staurr, from Proto-Germanic *stauraz.

From Old Norse starkr, from Proto-Germanic *starkuz, from Proto-Indo-European *sterg-.

From Old Norse stykki, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją.

From Old Norse stýra, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną.
From Old Norse stýri, from Proto-Germanic *stiuriją.

From Old Norse svanr (“swan”), from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”).

From Old Norse sveðja, from Proto-Germanic *swaþjǭ.

From Old Norse sveiti, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), *sweyd-.

From Old Norse svífa, from Proto-Germanic *swībaną.
From Old Norse svíi, from Proto-Germanic *swihô.
From Old Norse svíkva, svíkja, from Proto-Germanic *swīkwaną.

From Old Norse vinstri, from Proto-Germanic *winistraz. Cognates with Old High German winstar, Danish venstre and Swedish vänster.
From Old Norse vinr, Proto-Germanic *winiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to seek, desire, love, win”).

parole.significato: to harness (power or energy), to exploit
parole.testo: From Old Norse virkja, from Proto-Germanic *wirkijaną.
From Old Norse virða, from Proto-Germanic *wirþijaną. Related to verður (“valuable, worthy”).
From Old Norse visk, from Proto-Germanic *wiskō, a variant of *wiskaz.
From Old Norse visna, from Proto-Germanic *wisnon, *wesaną (“to consume”).
From Old Norse viss (“certain, sure”), from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz. Cognate with Swedish viss.
From Old Norse vit, from Proto-Germanic *witją. Cognate with Faroese vit, Danish vid, Swedish vett, English wit, Dutch wit, German Witz.
From Old Norse vita, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see”).
From Old Norse vitlauss, from Proto-Germanic *witjalausaz, whence also English witless. By surface analysis, vit (“wits, intellect”) + laus (“-less”).
From Old Norse vitni, from Proto-Germanic *witniją (“witness”).
From Old Norse vitr, from Proto-Germanic *witraz.
From Old Norse viðja, from Proto-Germanic *wiþjǭ. Related to Old Norse við (“withe”).
From Old Norse viðr, from Proto-Germanic *widuz.
From Old Norse váfa, from Proto-Germanic *wēbǭ.
From Old Norse vág, from Proto-Germanic *wēgō.
From Old Norse vágr, from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz.
From Old Norse valk, from Proto-Germanic *walką.
From Old Norse ván, from Proto-Germanic *wēniz.
From Old Norse vándr, from Proto-Germanic *wanh-.
From Old Norse vápn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną.
From Old Norse vátr, from Proto-Germanic *wētaz.

parole.significato: raiment, a piece cloth, weeds, clothing, garment, weave, fabric
parole.testo: From Old Norse váð, from Proto-Germanic *wēdiz, whence also Old English wǣd, Old Saxon wād, Old High German wāt. Cognate with Faroese váð and Swedish våd.
From Old Norse vá (whence also vo), from Proto-Germanic *waiwō and *wanhō.
From Old Norse vægi (“weight, moment”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgjō (“weight”), itself a derivative of *weganą (“to carry, weigh”).
From Old Norse vænta, from Proto-Germanic *wēnatjaną, related to *wēniz (“likely; hopeful”).
From Old Norse værr, possibly from Proto-Germanic *wēraz.
From Old Norse væta, from Proto-Germanic *wētijaną.
From Old Norse væta, from Proto-Germanic *wētijǭ.
From Old Norse vé, from Proto-Germanic *wīhą.
From Old Norse vér, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy, plural of *éǵh₂.
From Old Norse vídd, from Proto-Germanic *wīdiþō.
Derived from Old Norse víf, from Proto-Germanic *wībą.
From Old Norse víg, from Proto-Germanic *wīgą, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk-.

parole.significato: to consecrate, to set apart for a holy use; to dedicate to God
parole.testo: From Old Norse vígja and from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną.

parole.significato: a small bay, a cove, an inlet
parole.testo: From Old Norse vík, from Proto-Germanic *wīks.
From Old Norse víkva, víkja, from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną.

parole.significato: something in which alcohol or wine is stored in; a container of wine
parole.testo: Equivalent to vín (“wine”) + fat (“container”); from Old Norse vínfat, from Proto-Germanic *wīnafatą. Cognate with German Weinfass.
From Old Norse víss, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz.
From Old Norse vísdómr, from Proto-Germanic *wīsadōmaz. Equivalent to vís + -dómur. Cognate with Swedish visdom, English wisdom and German Weistum.
From Old Norse víta, from Proto-Germanic *wītaną.
From Old Norse víti, from Proto-Germanic *wītiją.
From Old Norse víxl, from Proto-Germanic *wihslaz. Cognate with Swedish växel, German Wechsel, Dutch wissel; compare also English wrixle.
From Old Norse víðir, from Proto-Germanic *wīþijō, from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis (“that which twines or bends, branch, switch”). Cognate to Dutch wijde (“willow”), Swedish vide.
From Old Norse víðr, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz.

parole.significato: a hole in the ice, a polynya
parole.testo: From Old Norse vǫk, from Proto-Germanic *wakwō.

From Old Norse vǫl (neuter plural or feminine singular). The word might be an Old Norse (or later Icelandic) alteration of an original neuter plural (the plural of val), since it is in Old Norse definitely attested in neuter plural but perhaps also in feminine singular, or else the feminine word is
From Old Norse vǫllr, from Proto-Germanic *walþuz. Cognate with Faroese vøllur, Norwegian voll, Old English weald (English weald, wold) and Old High German wald (German Wald).
From Old Norse vǫrr (“lip”), from Proto-Germanic *weruz (“lip”).
From Old Norse vǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *warīniz.
From Old Norse vǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *warduz.
From Old Norse vǫttr, from Proto-Germanic *wantuz.
From Old Norse vǫxtr, from Proto-Germanic *wahstuz.
From Old Norse vǫðvi, from Proto-Germanic *waþwô.
From Old Norse ydda (past tense yddi), from Proto-Germanic *uzdijaną, from *uzdaz (whence Icelandic oddur (“sharp tip, point”)).
From Old Norse yfir, from Proto-Germanic *ubiri, from Proto-Indo-European *upéri, from *upér, from *upo. Related to of (“too”) and ofan (“from above”).
From Old Norse yndi, from Proto-Germanic *wunjō.

parole.significato: to lift, raise (most often used of raising the shoulders or a hat)
parole.testo: From Old Norse yppa, from Proto-Germanic *uppijaną (“to raise, lift”).
From Old Norse ysta, from Proto-Germanic *justijaną.

parole.significato: your, yours (referring to one or more owners)
parole.testo: From Old Norse yðarr, yðvarr, from Proto-Germanic *izweraz.
From Old Norse á (“river”), from Proto-Germanic *ahwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”). Compare Danish å, Norwegian å, Swedish å.
From Old Norse ábyrgja from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną.
From Old Norse alfr, from Proto-Germanic *albiz, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós.
From Old Norse álka (“auk”), from Proto-Germanic *alkǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“a kind of bird”).

From Old Norse áll, from Proto-Germanic *ēlaz. The term is common Germanic, found in each Germanic dialect and absent outside. From Old Norse án, ón, from Proto-Germanic *ēnu.
From Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *airō. Cognates include: Old English ār (“oar”) (English oar).
Inherited from Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *airi. Cognates include: Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂 (air, “early”), Old English ār and ærlice (English early).
Inherited from Old Norse áss, from Proto-Germanic *ansaz.
From Old Norse áss, likely from Proto-Germanic *amsaz, cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌼𐍃 (ams, “shoulder”), but possibly the same as ás (1).

parole.significato: one of the Æsir, the principal Norse gods
parole.testo: From Old Norse áss, ǫ́ss, from Proto-Germanic *ansuz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂émsus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ens- (“to engender, beget”).

From Old Norse ást, from Proto-Germanic *anstiz. Cognate with Faroese ást, Norwegian Nynorsk åst, Old English æst, est (“consent, kindness, pleasure”), Old High German anst (“joy, favour, gratitude”), Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐍃𐍄𐍃 (ansts).
From Old Norse át, from Proto-Germanic *ētą.
From Old Norse átján, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Cognate with the Swedish arton, Danish atten, English eighteen and German achtzehn.
From Old Norse átt, from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz.
From Old Norse átta, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Norwegian åtte, Swedish åtta, Danish otte.
From Old Norse átti, from Proto-Germanic *ahtudô; now replaced with áttundi, a form influenced by sjöundi and níundi.
Inherited from Old Norse æ.
From Old Norse ǿgja, from Proto-Germanic *ōgijaną (“to frighten, to scare”), causative of *aganą (“to fear, to be scared”). Cognate with Old English onēġan, Gothic 𐍉𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ōgjan).

parole.significato: when traveling, to stop to rest or eat
parole.testo: From Old Norse æja, probably from a Proto-Germanic *ahjaną, related to Sanskrit अशनाति (aśnā́ti, “eat”), Ancient Greek ἄκολος (ákolos, “morsel”).
From Old Norse œmta, from Proto-Germanic *wōmatjaną.
From Old Norse œpa, from Proto-Germanic *wōpijaną.
Inherited from Old Norse ær, from Proto-Germanic *awiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis.
From Old Norse ǿrr, from Proto-Germanic *wōrijaz. Cognate to Old English wērig (modern weary).
From Old Norse æs, from Proto-Germanic *ansijō. Cognate with Latin ānsa (“handle”).

parole.significato: to excite, to stir up, rile (often with upp)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ǿsa, from Proto-Germanic *jōsijaną.
From Old Norse ǿska, ǿrskan, from Proto-Germanic *junhiskǭ.
From Old Norse œskja, from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną.
From Old Norse æta, from Proto-Germanic *ētijǭ.

parole.significato: to intend, to plan, to mean to, be going to
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ætla, from Proto-Germanic *ahtilōną (“to strive, think”). Cognate with Swedish ättla, Old Danish ætle.

parole.significato: family (referring to an extended family, dynasty, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ætt, from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz. Doublet of átt.
From Old Norse ætr, from Proto-Germanic *ētijaz.
From Old Norse ævi, from Proto-Germanic *aiwį̄.
From Old Norse œða, from Proto-Germanic *wōdijaną. Cognate with wüten.

From Old Norse ǿði f, from Proto-Germanic *wōdį̄; compare Faroese øði f. By surface analysis, óður (“furious, crazy”) + -i n (abstract noun). The shift in gender from feminine to neuter is presumably due to the influence of ǿði n (“mind, disposition”), for which see Etymology 3 below.
Inherited from Old Norse ǿði n (“mind, disposition”), from Proto-Germanic *wōþiją.

parole.significato: higher, greater, of a higher rank
parole.testo: From Old Norse œðri, probably from Proto-Germanic *wōþijaz.
From Old Norse æðr, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *ēdī, cognate with Sanskrit आति (āti, “aquatic bird”), or else from Proto-Germanic *awidō, cognate with Latin avis (“bird”).
Inherited from Old Norse æðr, from Proto-Germanic *ēdrǭ. Now replaced by the form æð.
Inherited from Old Norse œðr, from Proto-Germanic *wōdijaz. Now mostly replaced by the variant væður.
The Icelandic pronoun continues Old Norse ek, from Proto-Germanic *ek, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm. The pronoun is attested, in Proto-Norse inscriptions, since at least the 3rd century.
Common Germanic. From Old Norse eta, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.
From Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.
From Old Norse íkorni, from Proto-Germanic *aikwernô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer-.

From Old Norse eiskra (“rage before hot excitement”), from Proto-Germanic *aiskrōną (“to rage”), according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *aisk- (“shining, bright”), comparable to Proto-Slavic *jьskra (“spark”). However, compare *h₂ey- (“to energize, to invigorate”) and *h₂eydʰ- (“to ignite”).
From Old Norse ítr, from Proto-Germanic *ītraz.

From Old Norse ó-, ú-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, a prefix use of the particle *né (“not”). In Icelandic this changed very early from ú- to ó-. Cognate with Old English un- (English un-), Old Saxon un-, Dutch on-, Old High German un- (German un-), Swedish o-, Norwegian

From Old Norse ófreskja, from the adjective ófreskr (“clairvoyant”) and the noun ófreski (“clairvoyance, second sight”), of uncertain origin, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *unfriþiskaz (as per S. Bugge 1885), but according to F. Holthausen cognate with Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌸𐌹 (fraþi), then from *fraþiskaz.

From Old Norse úfriðr, from Proto-Germanic *unfriþuz. By surface analysis, ó- (“un-”) + friður (“peace”). From Old Norse ógn, from Proto-Germanic *ōgan-, deverbal of *ōgijaną (“to frighten, to scare”). More at ægja. Cognate of Old Swedish oghn (“fear, terror”).
From Old Norse óhreinn, from Proto-Germanic *unhrainiz; equivalent to ó- (“un-”) + hreinn (“clean”).
From Old Norse ál, from Proto-Germanic *anhulō.

From Old Norse úlíkr, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, ó- (“un-”) + líkur (“like”). Old English unġelīċ (English unlike), Dutch ongelijk, German ungleich, Swedish olik, Norwegian Bokmål ulik.
From Old Norse ómr, from Proto-Germanic *wōmaz.
From Old Norse órar (“fits of madness (plural)”), from Proto-Germanic *wōrō, related to Proto-Germanic *wōrijaz (“intoxicated”) (whence English weary).
From Old Norse óss, from Proto-Germanic *ōsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éh₁os (“mouth”), cognate with Old English ōr, Latin ōs (“mouth”).
From Old Norse ósk, from Proto-Germanic *wunskō, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).

parole.significato: the last part of the night before morning, roughly 3 a.m.; the start of the second of the eight eyktir
parole.testo: From Old Norse ótta from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ. Cognate with Old English ūhta, Old Saxon ūhta, Old High German ūhta, regional German Uchte (“midnight mass”), Norwegian Bokmål otte, and as the enhanced form Dutch ochtend (“morning”).

parole.significato: very bad weather; very stormy weather (usually with rain)
parole.testo: From Old Norse óveðr. Equivalent to ó- + veður. Cognate with English unweather and Danish uvejr, all from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą (“bad weather, storm”).
From Old Norse óðal, from Proto-Germanic *ōþalą.
From Old Norse óðr, from Proto-Germanic *wōdaz.
From Old Norse óðr, from Proto-Germanic *wōþaz.
From Old Norse ǫfund, from Proto-Germanic *abundiz (“jealousy, envy, resentment”).
Inherited from Old Norse ǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *ahanō.
From Old Norse ǫl (“ale, beer”), from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut-. Cognate with Swedish öl.
From Old Norse ǫld, from Proto-Germanic *aldiz.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *anadz (“duck, ennet”).
From Old Norse ǫnn, possibly from Proto-Germanic *azaniz.

Inherited from Old Norse ǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *arwaz.

From Old Norse ǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *arkō, from Latin arca.
From Old Norse ørlǫg, from Proto-Germanic *uzlagą.
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃or-no- (“eagle”). Cognate with Swedish örn.

Inherited from Old Norse ørvendr. The h comes from the mistaken association with the word hönd (“hand”). Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *uzwandijaną- attested by Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐍅𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (uswandjan, “to deviate”), Old English āwendan (“to turn away, turn the wrong way round”), and Old High German irwe
From Old Norse øx (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *akwisī, from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷs-ih₂- (“axe”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).
From Old Norse ǫxl, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō.
From Old Norse ǫðlingr, from Proto-Germanic *aþalaz (“noble”).

From Old Norse úlfaldi, from Proto-Germanic *ulbanduz (“camel”), borrowed from Latin elephantus (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφας (eléphas). Cognate with the Gothic 𐌿𐌻𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌿𐍃 (ulbandus, “camel”), Old English olfend (also as olfenda); Old High German olbento (“camel”).
From Old Norse ór (“out of”), from Proto-Germanic *uz (“out, out of”). More at Old English or-.
From Old Norse út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt.
From Old Norse útgangr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Equivalent to út + gangur. Cognate with Danish udgang, Swedish utgång, German Ausgang and English outgang.
From Old Norse úti, from Proto-Germanic *ūtai.
From Old Norse útlendr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandijaz.
From Old Norse útlenzkr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandiskaz.
From Old Norse ýla, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną.

parole.significato: the second month of winter according to the old Icelandic calendar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ýlir, from Proto-Germanic *jihwlijaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌾𐌹𐌿𐌻𐌴𐌹𐍃 (jiuleis, “a month”) and Old English ġiūli (“December and January(ærra géola ‘December’ & æfterra géola ‘January’(for & after))”).
From Old Norse ýsa, from Proto-Germanic *eusjǭ.
From Old Norse ýta, from Proto-Germanic *ūtijaną (“to push away”).
From Old Norse þak, from Proto-Germanic *þaką, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *teg-. Cognate with English thatch.
From Old Norse þakka, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną. Cognates include Faroese takka, Danish and Norwegian takke, Swedish tacka, English thank, Dutch danken and German danken.

From Old Norse þang, þongull, from Proto-Germanic *þangą, from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to thicken, be solid”), related to Proto-Germanic *þinhaną. Cognate with Swedish tång and Norwegian Bokmål tang.
From Old Norse þar, from Proto-Germanic *þar.
From Old Norse þari. Cognate with Faroese tari, Norwegian tare. Perhaps from a Proto-Germanic *þarhô, from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to twist”).
From Old Norse þarmr, from Proto-Germanic *þarmaz; whence Danish tarm. Cognate with German Darm, obsolete English tharms (“twisted guts”). Compare Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “hole”).
From Old Norse þat (“it, that”), from Proto-Germanic *þat, from Proto-Indo-European *tód (neuter of *só). Cognates include Swedish det, Faroese tað and English that.

From Old Norse þefa, from Proto-Germanic *þefōną, *þebōną (“to be hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *tep- (“warm; hot”). Cognate with Old English þefian (“to pant; be agitated”), Old English ofþefian (“to be exceedingly heated; be very hot”).
From Old Norse þefr (“smell, taste”), from Proto-Germanic *þafjaz.

parole.significato: to be silent, say nothing, hold one’s tongue
parole.testo: From Old Norse þegja, from Proto-Germanic *þagjaną. Cognate with Danish tie, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (þahan), Old High German dagēn, Latin taceō.
Inherited from Old Norse þegn, from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz. Cognate with English thane, German Degen.
From Old Norse þekja, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną.
From Old Norse þekkja, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng-.

parole.significato: underwool, the fine fur beneath the wool of sheep and similar animals
parole.testo: From Old Norse þel (“underwool”) from Proto-Germanic *þelą.

parole.significato: to stretch, spread out, draw (a bow)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þenja, from Proto-Germanic *þanjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“stretch”). Germanic cognates: Old Saxon þennian, Old High German dennen (German dehnen), Frankish *thinsan, Old Norse þenja (Norwegian tenja). parole.significato: this, that (referring to both persons and things)
parole.testo: From Old Norse [Term?] *þes-, þessi (neuter plural), sjá (nominative), related to and from the same ultimate origin as the irregular inflection of Old Norse sá, a descendant from the likewise irregularly inflected Proto-Germanic *sa. Cognate with Old English þes and Old High German dese.
From Old Norse þeyja, from Proto-Germanic *þawjaną.

parole.significato: thaw (warmth of weather sufficient to melt that which is frozen)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þeyr, from Proto-Germanic *þaujaz. Cognate with Faroese toyggjur, Norwegian tøyr.
From Old Norse þiggja, from Proto-Germanic *þigjaną.
From Old Norse þili, from Proto-Germanic *þilją. Related to Proto-Germanic *þelą.
From Old Norse þind, from Proto-Germanic *þendį̄.

From Old Norse þing (“assembly, council, business”), in turn from Proto-Germanic *þingą. Cognate with Faroese ting, Norwegian ting, Swedish ting, and Danish ting, English thing, Dutch ding, German Ding.
From Old Norse þinga, from Proto-Germanic *þingōną, from *þingą (“matter, issue”).
From Old Norse þistill, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz.
From Old Norse þjaka, þjökka, from Proto-Germanic *þakwōną. More at thwack.

parole.significato: to pain, plague, cause (one) to suffer
parole.testo: From Old Norse þjá, from older þéa, from Proto-Germanic *þewāną.
From Old Norse þjófr, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.
From Old Norse þjónusta, þjónasta, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz.

From Old Norse þjórr, from Proto-Germanic *þeuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros. Cognate with Faroese tjórur, Danish tyr and Swedish tjur, and more distantly with Ancient Greek ταῦρος (taûros) and Latin taurus. Doublet of tarfur, which was borrowed from Old Irish.
From Old Norse þjóta, from Proto-Germanic *þeutaną.
From Old Norse þjóð (“people, nation”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”).

From Old Norse þoka, from Proto-Germanic *þukōną; cognate with Danish tåge, Norwegian Bokmål tåke, Swedish töcken, Middle Low German dake, Old English *þuh (as in geþuxian (“to become dark, cloudy”)).

parole.significato: to endure, to take, to withstand
parole.testo: From Old Norse þola, from Proto-Germanic *þulāną. Cognate with Swedish tåla, Danish tåle, Norwegian Bokmål tåle, Norwegian Nynorsk tole, English thole.
From Old Norse þollr, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz.
From Old Norse þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą.

From Old Norse þorskr (“cod”) from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz. Cognates include Danish torsk, English torsk, Faroese toskur, German Dorsch, Irish trosc, Middle Dutch dorsch, Middle Low German dorsch, Norwegian torsk, Scottish Gaelic trosg and Swedish torsk.
From Old Norse þorsti, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz.
From Old Norse þraut, from Proto-Germanic *þrautō, *þrautą (“complaint, annoyance, struggle, swink”).
From Old Norse þrefa (“to wrangle; dispute”), from Proto-Germanic *þrebaną, related to Old English þrafian (“to quarrel”). More at thrave.

From Old Norse þreifa (“to touch, feel with the hand; feel for oneself, grope along”), from Proto-Germanic *þraibijaną, causative of *þrībaną (“to seize, take hold, prosper”), from Proto-Indo-European *terp-, *trep- (“to satisfy, enjoy”). Related to thrive.
From Old Norse þrek, from Proto-Germanic *þrakja-, from Proto-Indo-European *treg- (“strength”). Cognate with Old Saxon threki.
